# Raw Initializer External Slice Plan

The initial draft treated “the printer can emit it,” “the parser can accept it,” “the external file is readable,” and “the slice is still correct” as one thing. During review, separate these judgments first. They may meet in one model, but their failure points differ and should not be covered by the same success flag.

## Tradeoffs Retained from the Initial Draft

The first version proposed a large sample: the text graph would contain an initializer, and the model would reference a segment of data in an external file. This arrangement is convenient in practice. Readers only need to open one input to see the objects relevant to the compatibility window together.

The problem is that a large sample blurs the judgment. If the output text is accepted by the parser, that does not show that the initializer is still represented in its original form; if the external file can be opened, that does not show that the offset and length actually participate in the read. A slice that happens to cover the entire file can also make an implementation that ignores the range fields appear to work.

The original combined-sample proposal is therefore retained, but only as supporting material. It is responsible for preserving the combined scenario. Raw initializers and external slices should each have independent observation points, and neither may substitute for the other during review.

## The Initializer Track

Here, “raw initializer” is not a blanket term for all TensorProto; it refers to objects in the compatibility window that must not first be converted into display-friendly numeric forms and then be expected to have their original meaning guessed by the reader. int8 and float16 require particular care: the former’s signedness changes the meaning of elements, while the latter’s displayed values do not inherently represent the original storage units.

There are two options.

The first is to emit values that are easy to read at the output end and have the reader restore them based on type. The advantage is that the text is clear, and the scope of changes may be smaller. The problem is that once the output has flattened a type-specific distinction, the reader has no reliable information with which to restore it; eventual “read succeeded” status will mask the representation change.

The second is to have the output and reader use the same comparable representation for samples confirmed to require a raw round trip. This does not require changing every initializer to a low-level format, nor does it turn the two existing examples into a rule for all types. It only requires that retained sample content not be silently transformed during printing.

The current preference is the second option. The sample record should retain all three items: TensorProto from the input, the text actually produced by the printer, and TensorProto after reparsing. Looking only at the values shown on screen is insufficient, and retaining only a text segment is also insufficient. Element order must be checked as well, because a change in order will not always make the type or length immediately appear abnormal.

## The External Slice Track

An external slice should not be described broadly as “support for external data.” This round covers only ordinary external files inside the model directory, and whether the position and length in the metadata still denote the same content segment. Record file resolution and range interpretation separately.

The file-resolution question is whether the target can be located relative to the model directory. The range question is whether reading starts at the specified position and ends at the specified length. The former may hold while the latter is wrong; conversely, a correct expected fragment in memory does not show that the file entry point itself did not escape the directory.

An earlier investigation used `onnx/defs/parser.h` as the verification entry point. This location remains useful for adjacency navigation of text objects, but the path name does not show that it opens the external file, nor does it establish that the slice read happens there. Follow the actual references to confirm the file-handling entry point. Until then, the document retains only the navigation meaning of “start from the parser side.”

A quick check was suggested: read the entire external data into memory first, then compare it with the expected TensorProto. This can help inspect the final content, but it does not show whether offset and length were actually honored. If the entire file happens to match the expected content, or an incorrect range still lands on the same elements, the check may pass. Keep this approach for temporary diagnosis, not as an acceptance condition for this round.

Another approach is to confirm only that the target file exists. This is useful for finding a missing file or an incorrect model directory, but it likewise cannot replace the slice check. The new sample should make the target file larger than the required segment and make the full file and the specified segment produce different initializer results; otherwise, the range fields have not actually been observed.

## Scope for This Round

This round does not fold symlinks, parent-directory links, or other path cases into the slice sample. Those objects affect the boundary of file resolution, but the existing material does not say whether they should use the same conclusions as the range problem for ordinary files. Adding them merely to make the sample look complete would only mix path errors and range errors again.

Likewise, this page should not become a general description of the external-data mechanism. The objective is narrower: preserve the text-round-trip observation for raw initializers and allow the fact that the legacy call retains the external-slice result to be reviewed independently. If later investigation shows that the file entry point has no direct relationship to the parser path, narrow the navigation description here rather than forcing implementation ownership into it.

## Proceed or Withdraw

Prepare two independent samples before considering the combined sample. When the initializer sample fails, the record should state whether the change occurred in the printed text or in the read-back object. When the slice sample fails, the record should state whether the problem was file resolution, range interpretation, or a mismatch in the final read content. This way, even if the change lands in different locations, reviewers do not have to guess the cause from one large sample.

Withdrawal criteria should also be separate. If the raw initializer can only be read back by rewriting its existing representation, withdraw the text-round-trip portion and return to the format-selection discussion. If the external slice can pass only by ignoring the model directory, ignoring the position, or treating the entire file as the target segment, withdraw the slice portion; do not call that relaxation compatibility with the legacy call.

Three items remain to be decided: whether the existing samples should cover only the two initializer types mentioned so far; whether the combined model is still worth retaining once the independent samples are stable; and whether a type boundary still exists between the bytes read by the external slice and the interpretation of TensorProto that needs to be listed separately.

# Raw Initializer and External Slice Proposal

This record has been in the IR-18 compatibility window for a long time. It did not begin as a complete design, but as a review note tying together two easily overlooked observations: raw initializers still appeared readable after a text round trip; external data references still appeared able to open files. The problem that emerged later was not whether these two statements were entirely wrong, but that they made it too easy to stop at “readable” and “can be opened,” overlooking whether the objects and ranges were preserved.

The two subjects in the title can appear in the same model, but there is no reason to require them to share an implementation entry point, nor to let one regression result vouch for two sets of semantics. The raw initializer trail runs through the text printer, parser, and TensorProto; the external slice trail runs through the model directory, ordinary external files, positions, and lengths. An earlier investigation left `onnx/defs/parser.h` as a starting point. That starting point can still be used to find adjacent text-related objects, but is no longer treated as a basis for deciding where file handling belongs.

The early sections below have not been cleaned up into a description of the current state. The working assumptions from several follow-up notes, withdrawn shortcuts, and old samples have all been retained, because people may still encounter these approaches through old branches or links. The current proposal comes later; first, read it in the context of these records.

## 2023-06-26: The Initial Combined-Sample Idea

The first draft only aimed to preserve the raw initializer example from the user report, while also keeping sight of the fact that the old call preserved external slice results. At the time, the most direct approach was to prepare a combined model: the text graph would contain an initializer, and the model materials would also point to an external file. If the input could be parsed, the output could be parsed again, and content could be read from the file, that seemed sufficient to show that there was no obvious break in the compatibility window.

The thinking at the time was that a combined sample would be easier to review than two separate samples. There would be only one model and one reproduction environment; anyone tracing back from the output could see both the text objects and external references in the same place. That judgment still holds for “retaining a combined scenario,” but it later became clear that this could not carry the full burden of validation.

Another assumption in the first draft was that, since the parser could accept the printer's output, raw initializers were probably fine too. The “probably” here was not examined at the time. Acceptance of the text shows, at most, that the reader did not immediately reject it; it does not answer whether a type-related representation was replaced with another form during output, nor whether the elements of the object read back have the same meaning as those of the original object.

External slicing was also described too simply. The first draft treated “the external file is still readable” as a sign that slicing was still working. That judgment was later narrowed: finding the file is only one observation at the entry point, and does not show that reading starts at the specified position or ends at the specified length. If the sample happens to make the file length equal to the expected length, reading the entire file and slicing correctly could even produce the same result.

The initial draft did not promise that all TensorProto types would use the same textual form, nor did it promise to cover all external data paths. It left only one practical direction: first bring samples that expose differences into review, then decide where to make changes. This boundary remains in place today, avoiding turning a compatibility-window review sheet into an unreliable global account.

## 2023-10-31: Redrawing boundaries during review

The first formal review did not immediately decide to change the printer, parser, or external file entry point. The first change was to the unit of review: rather than treating “one model round-trips successfully” as the sole conclusion, the review was split into a raw-initializer track and an external-slice track, based on the questions readers needed answered.

The raw-initializer track needed to answer this question: given an existing TensorProto, after it passes through the text printer and is then read by the parser, does the resulting object still represent the same set of elements? At least two kinds of observations cannot substitute for each other here. The first is the output text, because the format itself may become what the reader actually sees; the second is the object read back, because acceptable text may still be interpreted as different values. Element order should also be examined in the same place; comparing only type names or element counts is not enough.

The external-slice track needed to answer this question: when an ordinary external file within the model directory is referenced, do the position and length still point to the segment expected by the old call? Here, too, there are two kinds of observations. Whether the file can be located is an entry-point issue; whether the range fields are interpreted is a reading issue. If both are described as “external data works normally,” then after a failure there is no way to know whether to start investigating the directory, the file, or the metadata.

The review did not separate the two tracks by directory or personnel. Their division came from failure modes, not from who was more likely to modify the code. The cost of this approach is that subsequent commits may touch different locations, and reviewers must read them separately; the benefit is that, merely to keep a change neatly unified, text changes will not be misclassified as file changes, nor will external file entry-point failures be misclassified as parser failures.

This review retained the combined sample but downgraded it to a reproduction scenario. Only if independent samples have already provided separate results for text round-tripping and range reading can the combined model show whether the two kinds of objects affect each other when they appear together. If it merely joins two examples that have already passed, the information it provides is insufficient to offset the maintenance cost.

## 2023-11-01: Gaps left by review comments

The post-review version did not interpret “raw” as arbitrary raw bytes, nor did it expand “external slices” into a comprehensive path-safety policy. The former focuses on ensuring that existing initializers within the compatibility window are not silently replaced in their textual representation by a convenience display; the latter focuses on ensuring that the file ranges old calls need to retain are not obscured by whole-file reads.

The annotations contain a question that was not resolved on the spot: should a sample record only the final TensorProto, or must it also record the printer's intermediate text? In the end, “keep only the result” was not chosen. The reason is simple: if the text itself has already lost the content that distinguishes representations, then even if the final object comparison happens to show equality, it cannot demonstrate that the format interface has not changed. Conversely, text alone cannot guarantee that the parser's interpretation has not deviated.

Another gap is exactly where the entry point for external files is. `onnx/defs/parser.h` was the first path found during the earlier investigation, and is a suitable starting point for searching outward from declarations and adjacent calls; however, no conclusions about opening file paths, directory boundaries, or range reads can be drawn from this filename alone. Places in the old version where “search from the parser side” was read as “determined by the parser” should now all be understood as navigation notes.

These annotations were not expanded into a call-chain diagram. Without sufficient material, drawing a complete chain would only create conclusions that are harder to clean up than the gaps themselves. The retained approach is: for text differences, start by examining objects adjacent to the parser; for external slice differences, first confirm the target file, position, and length separately. The actual processing entry point is determined by the results obtained by following references.

## Old approach retained from 2024: read the entire file before comparing

Someone once suggested first reading the entire external file into memory, then comparing it with the expected TensorProto content. This approach is tempting for temporary troubleshooting: it reduces variables in the file environment, and the final numerical values are easy to view side by side. Early records briefly described it as a shortcut implementation for external slice samples.

This approach is now marked as **deprecated**, but has not been deleted. The problem is not that reading into memory is necessarily wrong, but that it removes the observation of “whether the data is read as a slice.” If the implementation actually reads the entire file and then happens to obtain the same set of elements by other means, the content comparison may still pass. In that case, the sample can only prove that certain data can be obtained, not that offset and length still have semantic meaning.

The remaining value of the old approach is in investigating the file content itself. When file corruption, missing content, or an incorrect model directory is suspected, examining the entire file can help narrow the scope. However, it should not serve as grounds for adopting this proposal, nor should it be written into the regression materials as the sole pass condition. The current slice samples must produce distinguishable results for the complete file and the target segment.

Another old suggestion alongside this one was to confirm only that the external file exists. It has not been completely discarded either: whether the target is in the model directory and whether the file can be located are still among the first conditions to check. But “exists” only answers the entry-point question; it cannot replace the range question. If the document says only “the file can be opened,” readers should understand this as a limited observation, not a conclusion that the slice is correct.

## Another old practice retained from 2024: check only whether the text can be read again

The raw initializer once had a shorter check: feed the printer output back to the parser, and count it as a pass as long as it is accepted. This check is suitable for finding obvious lexical, delimiter, or formatting breaks, so early sample A is still retained in the old branch.

It cannot confirm that the original representation has been preserved. Accepting the text shows, at most, that lexical and syntactic checks did not reject it at the entry point; it cannot show whether signed integers are still interpreted with the same meaning, nor whether half-precision content still corresponds to the original storage units. If the output side first rewrites the information into another seemingly reasonable numeric value, the parser's success will make the problem harder to detect.

Therefore, old sample A can now serve only as a quick screening check. It can no longer independently support the conclusion that “initializer round trips are stable.” Whenever a judgment about the compatibility window is needed, the input object, the actual output text, and the read-back TensorProto must be retained side by side; if any one of the three is missing, only a narrower observational conclusion should be drawn.

This is not a proposal to change all initializers to a hard-to-read display format. The existing material is insufficient to establish a formatting strategy for all types. The review is limited to samples that already require preservation of their original representation; if other data types carry similar risks, those risks should be demonstrated through their own inputs, text, and read-back objects, rather than extrapolated from two examples.

## 2025-09-08: Blind spots found while organizing the old examples

During the cleanup, the design of the early samples was reexamined, rather than merely checking whether they remained in the repository. The gap in old example A is that it only checks whether printer output reenters the parser, without requiring the read-back TensorProto to be compared with the input object in the same place. It can still help detect obvious format breakage, but it cannot expose cases where “the text is readable, but the object has changed.”

The gap in old example B is that the external file's length is exactly equal to the expected read length. It is suitable for confirming that the minimal file can be found, but it cannot distinguish “reading by range” from “always reading the entire file.” Even if the implementation ignores the position and length, the result may happen to be the same. This example should not be deleted, because troubleshooting the old issue may still require it to identify a missing file; however, it can no longer be called a slice sample.

Taken together, the two old examples illustrate exactly why this page does not use a single pass indicator. A short sample does not mean it has little semantic content. Unless the variable being changed actually affects the result, the test is only confirming conditions that have not changed. The original initializer sample must make representation differences visible; the external slice sample must make the read range visible.

The cleanup also confirmed a boundary that remains unresolved: regular-file slicing is not the same issue as symbolic links or parent-directory links. The former first requires observing the range fields, while the latter first involves path boundaries. They may intersect in subsequent work on file entry points, but there is currently no material supporting their treatment as the same rule or the same category of failure. To avoid misleading readers, this page uses only regular files as the starting point for slice samples.

## A note from the review table

A seemingly simple question came up during the review: if the final numeric values are equal, why care about the original form? At the time, this was not turned into a slogan, but broken down into two concrete checks: whether the output text can express the same set of elements; and whether parsing it again yields the same kind of TensorProto interpretation. The former prevents the output stage from losing distinguishing information, while the latter prevents the reading stage from changing the interpretation.

Another question is whether path safety and slice correctness can be checked in one pass. The conclusion is not to combine the two, but to acknowledge that they fail at different points. When the target falls outside the model directory, the primary issue is the entry-point boundary; when the file is correct but the read range is wrong, the primary issue is metadata interpretation. A composite model can trigger these conditions at the same time, but error records and review conclusions should still be written separately.

There was also a suggestion at the time to “convert external slices to inline data, then let the text workflow handle everything uniformly”. It was not pursued further. Doing so would change the premise that existing calls retain external-slice results, and would also remove the file range from the observation scenario. If a future discussion concerns migration to inline data, this can be proposed again; within the current compatibility window, it is not a way to preserve existing behavior.

The review record did not develop these side notes into a complete explanation of the mechanism. Readers only need to be able to start investigating from three entry points: the raw initializer, the external slice, and `onnx/defs/parser.h`. Implementation ownership, call relationships, and error branches beyond these three objects should be confirmed at the specific references, not filled in ahead of time by this page.

## Current Options

There are two directions for raw initializers that can still be compared. Option one preserves existing output conventions and puts compatibility on the reading side as much as possible. Its advantage is that the surface area of changes is concentrated, and the existing output path appears unaffected; the risk is that if the output has already rewritten the original information, the reading side can only interpret what remains and cannot reliably recover distinctions that were never written down.

Option two targets only the initializers already confirmed to require round-tripping within the scope of this review, and explicitly requires output and input to preserve the same set of comparable representations. It makes the format an interface surface that needs review, and also requires samples to check both text and objects. The cost is that compilation or simple parsing alone is not enough; the benefit is that it is easier to identify whether a failure occurs during output or reading.

There are also two directions for external slices. The first compares only the final content read, with low preparation cost, but cannot establish whether the offset and length are still respected. The second makes the external file larger than the target segment and ensures that the full file and the target range produce different results. The second requires a little more sample preparation, but can directly distinguish whole-file reads from specified-range reads.

The current preference is for option two for initializer handling, and the second type of external-slice sample. Here, “preference” is not a decision on all implementation details. The actual entry point for opening files, how failure information needs to be presented, and whether to include the directory boundary in the same round of changes all still depend on subsequent references and samples. At this point, the proposal only establishes the observation points that should not be sacrificed for convenience.

## Materials to Retain Before Adoption

Raw-initializer samples should retain the input object, printer output, and read-back TensorProto in adjacent locations. The record does not need to become a long log, but it cannot retain only “passed”. If the output text can no longer distinguish the representations that originally needed to be preserved, the text surface cannot be considered stable, even if the value displayed by a particular runtime looks close.

External-slice samples should clearly specify the target file in the model directory, as well as the fact that the referenced range is not the entire file. This does not require one example to cover all path boundaries; it only requires the sample to produce different results for “reading the entire file” and “reading the specified segment”. If the record only proves that the file was found, the conclusion can only state that the file entry point is usable; if the record only proves that the final content is the same, the conclusion cannot be extended to claim that the range fields have been covered.

The two samples should be able to fail independently. When the initializer fails, it should be possible to tell whether the difference is in the text, the element order, or the round-tripped object. When slicing fails, it should be possible to tell whether the problem is file resolution, the offset, the length, or the resulting content. This will not reduce the number of subsequent changes, but it will prevent one large sample from collapsing different failures into a single failure that is difficult to review.

## Current proposal

The current proposal imposes preservation requirements on only two interface surfaces. The first is the original initializer's text round trip: the output must retain enough information for the reader to restore the same object, and the check covers both the actual text and the round-tripped TensorProto. The second is external slicing: when ordinary external files are referenced within the model directory, the sample must make the interpretation of the offset and length independently observable; file readability cannot substitute for range correctness.

The original initializer's public text format must preserve the signed int8 sequence {1,-2,127,-128} and the float16 bit patterns {15360,49152,14336}; the TensorProto values obtained by parsing them again must not change.

This requirement only covers the original initializer samples explicitly identified in this review. It does not claim that all data types should use the same textual format, nor does it bring all external-data cases into this page. int8 must preserve the signed decimal meaning of its elements; float16 must preserve its 16 storage bit pattern; after reparsing, neither may change because the output selected a different presentation.

External slicing remains subject to a narrower scope. Samples using ordinary files come before symlinks and parent-directory links; file entries come before broader path rules; and the offset and length come before inferences about all TensorProto external encodings. This ordering is not intended to delay the issue, but to ensure that each sample actually answers the question it was designed to answer.

## Fallback points if not adopted

If the initializer can only be read again by changing its existing representation, the text round-trip portion should not be included in the compatibility window; the format choice should be reconsidered. “Reading a value that is close” cannot be treated as preserving the original representation.

If external slicing can pass only by ignoring the model directory, treating the offset or length as optional information, or treating the entire file as the target content, the slicing portion should be withdrawn. Such a relaxation would change the premise for the scope retained for old calls and cannot be presented as compatibility.

If following the reference reveals that `onnx/defs/parser.h` only provides declaration navigation unrelated to this, the wording here about it should be narrowed further to an old troubleshooting entry point; it should no longer imply that it contains the implementation for text reading or file handling. This condition does not change the requirements for the original initializer or external slicing themselves; it only prevents the documentation from miswriting a starting point as an ownership conclusion.

## Adjacent issues still open

Whether a combined sample is needed has still not been decided. Independent samples can already expose text round-tripping and range interpretation separately; a combined sample is worth maintaining only if it can show that the two genuinely affect each other. If it merely puts two already-passing examples into the same model, the incremental information is limited.

Whether symlinks and parent-directory links need to be listed separately after ordinary file slicing has also not been decided on this page. Those cases concern path boundaries, and a conclusion cannot be inferred from ordinary-file samples merely because the same words, “external file,” appear.

Finally, one question remains unanswered: after the bytes read by slicing enter initializer interpretation, are there boundaries that need to be listed separately by type? The current proposal only requires that a comparable TensorProto ultimately be observable; it does not assume that all types or all external encoding forms are already covered. Retaining this question avoids later misreading “range correctness” as meaning that all external representations of initializers have already been handled.

# Lexical and locale node-attribute troubleshooting tree

When graph text fails to read and node attributes appear to be missing, record them as two separate symptoms first; don't classify them together at the first step. The old troubleshooting lead is at `onnx/defs/parser.h`; this records the branches that the IR-18 sample could take at the time, not a complete reading guide.

The initial working assumption was that failures around special floating-point values were probably related to locale. After switching the environment to a setting that uses a period as the decimal separator, the text at hand did proceed further once. This only shows that the environment change affected that text; it does not show that quotes, comments, and whitespace are irrelevant. If graph, input, or output names are quoted, preserve them as-is first. Also don't remove comments or extra whitespace just to make reproduction easier.

```text
Read failure
├─ Cannot yet confirm that a node was formed
│  ├─ Text contains quoted identifiers
│  │  └─ Keep the complete fragment before and after the name
│  ├─ Text contains comments or extra whitespace
│  │  └─ Don't format it first; record the location of the anomaly
│  └─ Anomaly is near a special floating-point token
│     └─ Record the locale and the original lexeme
│
└─ A node exists, but its attributes do not appear as expected
   ├─ Save the node text and attribute section
   └─ First confirm that the node was not produced from normalized input
```

At the time, people would replace special values with ordinary numbers and then check whether the node appeared. This can expose a later path, but it cannot determine whether the original text stopped at lexical recognition, numeric conversion, or attribute reading. In particular, don't record success with the replacement as proof that the original input passed.

`inf` must be preserved as the original lexeme; don't change it to another numeric form in the record. If only formatted text remains, it is impossible to determine which lexical boundary it originally occupied.

Stop conditions: if there is no original graph text, no actual locale, or no way to confirm that the failure occurred before node formation, stop at the lexical branch. If the node fragment and attribute section are missing, don't guess the attribute names or default values.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Lexing and Locale-Related Node Attributes

This record still starts from `onnx/defs/parser.h`, but after review it no longer treats that as the source of every anomaly. Two types of descriptions often arrive together: one says the graph text stalls while being read, and the other says the text can already produce nodes, only for the attributes to turn out wrong afterward. Both descriptions mention quotes, comments, whitespace, and special floating-point forms, so the early handling merged them into a single path.

## Sequence Left by the Old Page

The old rule for the year 2023 was to switch locale first and then clean up the input. It came from text that, after an environment change, no longer failed at the same point; later, removing comments, collapsing whitespace, and stripping quotes from names were added to the same operation.

```text
Old approach
├─ Switch locale
├─ Remove comments
├─ Normalize extra whitespace
├─ Remove outer quotes from identifiers
└─ Check node attributes if processing continues
```

This sequence can no longer be used to determine the cause, but it is being retained temporarily. When all four actions happen at once, we only know that the rewritten text proceeded to a different point; we cannot tell which action moved the failure position. Removing quotes changes the lexical boundary of a name; deleting comments and collapsing whitespace also change how adjacent text is separated. Calling all of these changes a “locale fix” was the clearest over-attribution on the old page.

Another old conclusion also needs to be retained and flagged: after the text passes through the read entry point, the remaining issue is an attribute-read problem. The review found that this skips two observation points: whether a node has formed, and whether the formed node came from the same unmodified input. Reaching the entry point does not mean a node is available for attribute reads; a node appearing does not mean that the preceding lexical conditions did not affect the result.

## Duty-Shift Addendum

During the duty-shift review, the process changed to recording the evidence first and choosing the branch afterward. If a node has not yet been obtained, save only the original graph text, the fragment near the failure, the actual locale, and the error text. If a node already exists but its attributes do not match expectations, also save the node fragment and the attribute section. Do not merge the two cases under “attribute not read,” because that could mean the node did not form, an attribute is missing, an attribute value is abnormal, or reading stopped near the attributes.

Quoted graph, input, and output identifiers must not be renamed first. They may not be the cause of the anomaly, but manually removing the quotes destroys the boundaries in the original text. The same applies to comments: the input after deletion can be kept as a comparison, but it cannot replace the text present when the anomaly occurred. If extra whitespace is absorbed by a formatting tool, a node fragment seen later no longer necessarily corresponds to the verbatim input.

At the time, there was an attempt to replace special floating-point notation with ordinary decimal values and then check whether the attributes appeared. That experiment did not produce a directly usable determination. The numeric replacement changes both lexeme classification and numeric interpretation; even if the node then exists, that does not allow us to infer that the original lexeme was read correctly. Therefore, the result after replacement is recorded only as “rewritten sample continued,” not as evidence that the original issue was located.

## A Reproduction That Did Not Separate the Symptoms

One reproduction changed only the locale and left the rest of the text unchanged. The result did not reliably split the symptoms into two groups: some text still stalled near comments or whitespace, while some text reached the node stage and only then showed attribute differences. The evidence from that run was insufficient to assign the cause to either the lexical branch or the attribute branch.

This does not mean that locale has been ruled out. It only shows that changing the environment alone did not make the observed symptoms split consistently. The old record interpreted this failure as “the environment is not a factor”; that wording is no longer used. Likewise, we cannot write that the environment still has an effect as though that had been proven.

Another issue exposed by the reproduction was that the source of the node fragment was not always recorded clearly. Some checks were performed after comments were deleted, and others after quotes were removed from names. The resulting nodes can help locate sensitive positions, but they cannot be compared directly with the original failure. If the node did not come from the same original text, differences in attribute reads should not be used to explain the original text.

## Troubleshooting Tree Now in Use

```text
Graph-text anomaly or node-attribute anomaly found
│
├─ Node formation not confirmed
│  ├─ Anomaly near a quoted name
│  │  └─ Save the name, surrounding whitespace, and adjacent text; do not rename it first
│  ├─ Anomaly near a comment or extra whitespace
│  │  └─ Preserve the original segment; perform deletion or normalization only as a separate comparison
│  ├─ Anomaly near a special floating-point token
│  │  └─ Record the actual locale and the verbatim lexeme; do not overwrite it with an ordinary numeric value
│  └─ Failure position unclear
│     └─ First confirm whether the node has formed; if that cannot be confirmed, stay in this branch
│
└─ Node obtained, but attribute result is wrong
   ├─ Node came from unmodified input
   │  ├─ Save the node fragment and the attribute section
   │  └─ Record missing attributes, anomalous values, and read interruptions separately
   ├─ Node came from normalized text
   │  └─ Save it as a new sample; do not directly attribute the original anomaly to it
   └─ Only an oral description is available, with no node fragment
      └─ Stop; do not guess the attribute name
```

“Node obtained” in the tree is a stopping point, not a claim about implementation layers. Until that point has been crossed, chasing attribute names usually makes the record mix the earlier and later symptoms together. Conversely, once a node has appeared, do not simply go back to adjusting the locale; first confirm that the node text and attribute section still came from the same verbatim input.

## Gaps Retained During Review

The review did not require the old steps to be deleted. Someone may still reach this page through the old “switch locale” clue, so the old handling is retained, but it may only be used to identify historical samples and cannot independently support a new attribution. Environment changes, comment deletion, whitespace normalization, quote changes, and numeric replacement are different input conditions and cannot be collapsed into a single success or failure.

There are still unresolved parts of node-attribute reading: once the text has passed the previous stage, this record has no evidence to determine which attribute differences come from the original text and which come from the interpretation performed during reading. Future samples should save the failure text or output bytes and explicitly record whether the node formed. If the evidence only supports saying that “lexing and attribute reading have not yet been separated,” stop there; do not write either side as a confirmed cause.

# Lexical and locale Node-Attribute Troubleshooting Tree

This page was originally treated as a broad entry point: anything where the graph text could not be read, or where a node already appeared to exist but its attributes did not appear as expected, was sent here. The two symptoms look similar on the surface and often involve quoted names, comments, extra whitespace, and special floating-point notation; old records therefore referred to them as the same kind of “parse anomaly.” This page still retains that old entry point and wording because troubleshooters will follow it to find past samples, not because the old wording is precise enough.

The path that can still be checked directly is `onnx/defs/parser.h`. In early materials, it was simply a navigation point where lexical issues and node-attribute issues met. Do not assume from this path alone that all attribute anomalies are handled in the same place, and do not skip the input text just because the issue name contains “attribute.” Start by answering a smaller question on site: when the anomaly occurred, had a node already been formed from the input as-is?

What follows is a troubleshooting record annotated year by year. The old content has not beenwholereasoned into the current specification, and some paragraphs no longer apply; they can still explain why the later rule was to preserve the sample first and then perform a one-variable comparison.

## 2023-06: The Original Working Rule

The earliest text received stopped near a special floating-point value. The observation at the time was that after switching to a locale that uses a period as the decimal separator, the text no longer stopped at the same place. The old page therefore identified locale as the primary cause and gave a quick but insufficiently controlled sequence:

```text
Text read error
├─ Switch locale
├─ Remove comments
├─ Collapse extra whitespace
├─ Remove quotes around names
└─ Check node attributes if processing continues
```

The practical purpose of this sequence was to let people see the later node fragment as quickly as possible; that is also where its problem lies. The environment and the input were changed at the same time, so any instance of “continuing” only shows that the rewritten text reached the next stage. It cannot show that the original anomaly disappeared, nor that locale was the first thing to have an effect.

Removing quotes is not harmless cleanup. The symbols around graph, input, and output names determine where an identifier begins and ends. Removing comments is not harmless cleanup either: the position of a comment relative to an adjacent identifier or value is precisely the text boundary that needs to be observed. Collapsing extra whitespace into a uniform format also changes the input. The old rule performed all these actions together, so it could not distinguish which action changed the symptom.

An early record also contains a sentence that was later often quoted: “Once past the read entry point, everything else is an attribute issue.” At the time, this was meant to remind troubleshooters not to keep focusing on the environment, but it prematurely collapsed several observation points into one. Text entering an entry point, a node being constructed, and an attribute being read each require different evidence. Without an intermediate fragment, one cannot infer from “the error is not at the beginning” that a node has already formed, nor from “the attribute cannot be seen” that attribute reading definitely executed.

This version of the old rule was not deleted because some historical reproductions left only its keywords. When you see the clue “switch locale first” now, read it as an old experiment, not as a current determination criterion.

## Handwritten Notes Beside Old Samples

Later, a simple constraint was added in the margin of the old page: do not save a cleaned-up version of the text first. If a quoted name is manually renamed, its original lexical boundaries are lost; if comments are deleted before saving, their relationship to the surrounding lexemes cannot be recovered; if whitespace is absorbed by a formatting tool, there is also no way to know exactly what the input looked like when the anomaly occurred.

This addendum did not propose a complete procedure; it only required keeping the original text. Its starting point was not to assume that every quotation mark, comment, or whitespace character was a cause, but to avoid deleting potentially relevant boundaries at the outset. Once the original text has been preserved, comparisons can still be made by removing quotation marks, deleting comments, or cleaning up whitespace; however, each comparison must become a new sample and must not be written back as the original input.

Special floating-point forms were also treated as ordinary strings during this period. Some people would first replace them with a conventional numeric value to see whether the node could still appear. This often advanced the investigation to the subsequent node layer, but the replacement changed both lexical recognition and numeric interpretation. Even if attributes appeared afterward, that could not establish retrospectively that the original form had been accepted correctly. The description on the old page, “works normally after replacing it with an ordinary number,” only indicates that processing continued with the replacement text.

To avoid missing this detail, a margin note required anomalies near lexical processing to include at least the verbatim lexeme and the actual locale in the same record. Merely writing “floating-point issue” is meaningless; merely writing “worked after changing the environment” is also meaningless. Both shortcuts mix together the input, the environment, and the subsequent node behavior.

## A reproduction attempt that did not separate the issues

The subsequent reproduction attempt changed only the locale, leaving the rest of the text unchanged. The results did not produce a clean dividing line: some texts still stopped near comments or whitespace, while others reached node reading before showing differences in attributes. That round of observations did not provide enough material to attribute the cause to either branch.

This reproduction attempt was later misread as supporting two opposite conclusions. One claim was “locale has been ruled out”; the other was “locale has been confirmed as the sole factor.” Both claims went beyond what was recorded at the time. Switching the environment alone did not consistently separate the observed behavior into purely lexical and purely attribute-related categories; it only showed that this condition change itself did not provide enough distinction.

There was another, more practical gap in the reproduction attempt: node snippets were not always taken from the same input. Some checks deleted comments first, some removed quotation marks around names first, and some replaced special numeric values with ordinary numbers first. The resulting node outputs could help locate the next place worth examining, but they could not be placed alongside the original anomaly to make a causal judgment. Once the input had changed, the node and attribute results represented a different sample.

Therefore, later records split “the node appears” into two questions: whether the node appears, and whether it comes from the unmodified original text. The former can only determine whether to turn temporarily to the attribute branch; the latter determines whether that node can be used for comparison with the original anomaly. The old page did not make this distinction, leaving many judgments that “the attributes have already been verified” impossible to trace back.

## 2024-02: Classification after the on-call review

The on-call review revised the records to preserve the material first, then decide the next step. If there is no evidence that a node has already formed, follow the lexical branch first: save the original graph text, the snippets before and after the anomaly, the actual locale, and the failing text. If a node already exists but the attribute results do not meet expectations, follow the attribute branch: save the node snippet and the attribute section, and note whether these snippets come from the unmodified input.

This does not mean splitting the problem into two mutually unrelated implementation modules. A sample may be sensitive at a lexical boundary and may also show an attribute difference after a node is formed. The purpose of recording them separately is simply to avoid substituting a description from the later stage for the earlier stage when the earlier stage has not been confirmed. Whether the text actually forms a node is the most useful stopping point during on-call investigation.

“Attribute not read” has been split into separate cases in this version. It may mean that the attribute is completely missing, that the attribute value does not meet expectations, or that reading was interrupted near the attribute. Without a node fragment, it is difficult to distinguish even these three cases. Old records habitually wrote them as one sentence; after review, that sentence may no longer be used to directly infer the attribute name, default value, or read order.

The review also retained the previous cautious stance toward locale. The actual locale must be recorded together with the corresponding text; an environment description cannot be added afterward based on memory. A failure near a numeric form, without environment information, cannot be attributed to numeric semantics; if the symptom disappears after the environment changes, that result cannot be used to overwrite the original failure. The environment is an experimental condition, not an explanation that is automatically valid.

## Retained Legacy Handling

> Legacy handling, now for historical reference only: first replace the special floating-point notation with ordinary numbers; if a node appears, switch to checking attributes; if it is still stuck, adjust the locale.

This handling is no longer applicable. It treated “a node appears after replacement” as evidence that the original text had passed through the lexical stage, and treated “it still fails after replacement” as evidence that the environment had not been configured correctly. The first inference ignores the fact that the input has changed; the latter ignores that the failure location has not yet been confirmed.

The legacy handling was not deleted because it explains why two similar but non-identical texts appear in later samples: one retains the special floating-point term, while the other rewrites it as an ordinary numeric value. They can be placed under the same event, but they cannot substitute for each other in the record. If only the rewritten sample remains later, it is possible to say only that the subsequent path was observed; a conclusion about the original text cannot be added.

Likewise, the old practice of cleaning up comments and whitespace before inspecting attributes can still be used as a quick way to locate sensitive areas, but the result must be marked as cleaned-up input. It cannot prove that the lexical boundary of the original text is irrelevant, nor can it prove that attribute reading works normally for the original text.

## Limitations in Review

The review did not require this page to be expanded into an explanation of all parser behavior. The current event concerns the boundary involving lexical processing and locale, quoted identifiers, comments, extra whitespace, special floating-point literals, and node-attribute reading. During investigation, preserving these categories of input clues first is enough to avoid most mixed records; in the absence of evidence, there is no need to fill the gaps with a complete set of grammar rules.

The review also rejected another approach: first establish a baseline from formatted “normal text,” then infer the original text backward from that baseline. Formatting itself removes local conditions such as quotation marks, comment positions, and whitespace boundaries. Normal text can serve as an independent comparison, but it cannot replace the original failed sample, much less be called an equivalent copy of the anomalous input.

On-call personnel need to distinguish two stopping conditions in particular. First, if the original text or actual locale is unavailable, or it cannot be confirmed whether a node exists, stop at the lexical branch. Second, if the node fragment was not obtained from the original, unmodified input, or if there is no attribute portion, stop at the attribute branch. Stopping does not mean that the anomaly has been ignored; it means that the existing records are insufficient to support a stronger attribution.

The principle left after review is deliberately narrow: each comparison changes only one class of condition. Removing quotes, deleting comments, normalizing whitespace, switching the locale, and replacing special numeric values are separate actions. If multiple actions occur at the same time, the record can only say “the rewritten input changed”; it cannot single out one action as the cause.

## On-site Troubleshooting Tree

The tree below preserves this page’s original runbook purpose. It does not describe the complete reading process; instead, it specifies what to record first when an anomaly occurs, when a different branch may be tried, and when to stop.

```text
Anomaly found in graph text, or abnormal node attribute result
│
├─ A. Node formation has not yet been confirmed
│  │
│  ├─ A1. Anomaly is near a quoted graph, input, or output identifier
│  │  ├─ Save the name and the complete text before and after it
│  │  ├─ Do not remove the quotes first or change it to a shorthand name first
│  │  └─ If the phenomenon changes after only removing the quotes: save it as a comparison, and remain at the lexical boundary
│  │
│  ├─ A2. Anomaly is near a comment or excess whitespace
│  │  ├─ Save the original segment containing the adjacent text
│  │  ├─ Delete comments and normalize whitespace in two separate comparisons
│  │  └─ If both have already been changed at the same time: do not compare attributes; record that the input was rewritten
│  │
│  ├─ A3. Anomaly is near a special floating-point literal
│  │  ├─ Save the original lexeme and the actual locale
│  │  ├─ Do not overwrite the original lexeme with an ordinary numeric value
│  │  └─ If the original lexeme cannot be preserved: do not determine whether the literal was accepted
│  │
│  └─ A4. Failure location is unclear
│     └─ First confirm whether a node has been constructed; if this cannot be confirmed, do not move to B
│
└─ B. A node was obtained, but the attribute result does not meet expectations
   │
   ├─ B1. Node comes from unmodified original text
   │  ├─ Save the node fragment and the attribute section
   │  ├─ Record separately whether the attribute is missing, the value is abnormal, or reading was interrupted
   │  └─ If A material is also available, preserve the input association between the two
   │
   ├─ B2. Node comes from manually cleaned text
   │  ├─ Save it as a separate sample
   │  └─ Do not use it to explain the original text; return to A if necessary
   │
   └─ B3. Only a description that “the attribute was not read” is available
      └─ Stop when there is no node fragment or attribute section; do not guess the attribute name
```

A and B are recording branches, not a commitment about the internal layers of the code. The key point in A is whether the text has formed a node; the key point in B is whether the node and attribute section can be traced back to the same input. A sample may ultimately proceed from A to B, but discussing attributes at the end does not allow the original phenomenon from stage A to be erased.

### A branch: Preserve the lexical boundary first

When entering A, save the original graph text first, rather than a cleaned-up reproduction. The fragment should cover the identifiers, comments, whitespace, and numeric regions near the anomaly. There is no need to create another tidier example just for the record; real anomalies often occur precisely at boundaries that disappear during cleanup.

If the text contains a quoted name, retaining only the name itself is not enough; the text immediately before and after it must also be retained. A comparison with only the quotation marks removed can help determine whether the boundary is sensitive, but if that comparison passes, the conclusion can only be that the positions related to quotation marks warrant further review. It cannot automatically show that locale is correct, nor can it show that the node-attribute branch is irrelevant.

If a comment is immediately adjacent to an identifier or numeric value, first preserve the comment's original position, then perform a comparison that only removes the comment. If the behavior changes after removal, the original failing text must still remain in the record. The text after removal is not the “actual input,” but an explicitly rewritten comparison. Whitespace normalization follows the same principle: if the input continues to work after compression, that only shows that the boundary is format-sensitive; it cannot show which pair of adjacent lexemes caused the problem.

The locale record must remain attached to the specific sample. Without environment information, do not infer numeric rules from an error near a floating-point value; after switching environments, continued success with the text must not override the original anomaly. A recurring misuse on the old page is to write “locale changed” as the closing conclusion, when in fact it is only a change in conditions.

If branch A cannot obtain the original text or locale, or cannot confirm whether the node has been constructed, stop at A. At that point, the most valuable material is not a guess about some attribute-reading behavior, but the complete text fragment and the actual failure position. When someone obtains a new sample later, they should also keep the new sample separate from the old gap, rather than using the new input to fill in details that the old input did not record.

### Branch B: The node and attributes must come from the same input

Before entering B, first ask whether the node was obtained from unmodified text. If comments were deleted, quotation marks changed, whitespace folded, or numeric values replaced to make reading continue, that node can represent only the rewritten sample. It may still help with subsequent localization, but it cannot prove that attribute reading was functioning correctly in the original anomaly.

Branch B focuses on preserving the node fragment and the attribute portion. The record does not need to immediately determine whether the attribute issue is lexical, related to reading, or related to subsequent interpretation; first record “the node exists” and “the attribute result is not as expected” as two independent observations. A missing attribute, an abnormal attribute value, and an interruption during reading are different phenomena and must not be uniformly shortened to “the attribute was not read.”

Only when the same original text can show both the node's occurrence and the attribute anomaly may the two be compared side by side. Even then, do not directly declare that the preceding lexical condition is irrelevant. The lexical boundary may determine the range of the subsequent node text; attribute reading occurs later. Whether the two are related requires support from the same material and cannot be replaced by the issue title.

Branch B also has a conservative stopping point: when there is no node fragment, no attribute portion, or the input source has already changed, do not fill in a missing attribute name, default behavior, or reading order. Older records added speculation at this point, which later could not be checked against the original sample, so it is no longer used.

## Current guidance stated later

The parser must accept quoted graph, input, and output identifiers, comments, and extra whitespace, and must still parse special floating-point literals such as inf according to the published syntax when the locale uses a comma as the decimal separator; the similar but invalid inf1 must still be rejected.

This requirement separates the experience recorded on the old page—“change the locale first” and “clean up the text first”—from the actual syntax boundaries that must be preserved. For quoted names, comments, and extra whitespace, do not delete or format them first to obtain an apparent pass and then record the rewritten result as acceptance of the original text. For special floating-point literals, likewise do not replace them with ordinary numbers first, bypass reading, and then claim that the syntax as written is covered.When valid text is encountered but reading cannot continue, first return to branch A and save the raw input and locale. If a similar but invalid form is allowed through, likewise retain the actual text and stop at the lexical branch; do not rewrite it as a node-attribute event. Only after confirming that the node was constructed from unmodified text should you enter branch B to record the attribute behavior.

The current guidance here does not prescribe all behavior after reading node attributes. It only describes the public syntax boundary adjacent to this page and provides a way to distinguish lexical material from attribute material without conflating them in the field. `onnx/defs/parser.h` remains the verification entry point for the old record, but the path alone cannot assign all attribute-related behavior to the same implementation location.

## Adjacent issues not yet separated out

The user-facing entry point for reading node attributes may still collapse several different phenomena into the same description: sometimes the node never forms at all, sometimes the node has formed but its attribute portion is incomplete, and sometimes the record retains only a result without a node fragment. The current material is insufficient to prescribe uniform follow-up behavior for these cases, and they should not be forcibly merged into the lexical rules.

If samples are added later, prioritize retaining two types of material. ### Appendix A: Quick cleanup method (deprecated)

When old samples were anomalous, someone once first deleted comments and extra whitespace, then removed the outer symbols around quoted names. If the text could then continue to be read, the remaining differences were attributed to attributes. This method is quick when tidying failure screenshots, but it changes the lexical boundaries of the input. It is retained as a historical record and must no longer be used to determine the original issue.

### Appendix B: Numeric substitution method (deprecated)

Another old method was to change special floating-point text into an ordinary numeric value to confirm whether the node could appear. It can help determine whether there are other anomalies later in the path, but it cannot prove that the original numeric text was correctly recognized. The old page once described “node appears after substitution” as a successful read; that conclusion was later retracted.

### Appendix C: Empty items left by the old checklist

- Whether the raw input retained quotes, comments, and extra whitespace:
- Whether the actual locale was saved together with the failed text:
- Whether the node was constructed from unmodified input:
- Whether the attribute fragment can be traced back to the same input:
- Whether the anomaly description refers to missing data, an anomalous value, or a reading interruption:

The public inlining interface is `onnx.inliner.inline_local_functions(model: ModelProto, convert_version: bool = False) -> ModelProto`. It returns a new model without modifying the input; it recursively inlines opset-compatible local functions and removes expanded definitions. The default, False, retains functions and calls with a ONNX opset mismatch; True attempts to convert the function body from its ONNX opset to the model opset before inlining, preserving the semantics of the converted graph (the legacy ReduceLogSum axes attribute becomes an input supplied by a Constant, and the original attribute is removed). The tuples in `inline_selected_functions(model, function_ids: list[tuple[str,str]], exclude: bool = False)` are domain/name; False expands selected functions, and True expands unselected functions. The first can easily focus only on the function body; the second requires returning to the call sites in the same model and recording, in order, the local function inputs and outputs, symbolic dimensions, nodes after attribute binding, and whether data_prop propagated data to the required locations. domain and overload are recorded alongside these because they determine which function declaration is actually connected.

The old notes marked a function as passing as long as its output had a shape. That criterion has been corrected: the presence of a shape does not establish that the element type stays consistent or that a second processing pass still resolves to the same declaration. ONX-205 are retained as entry points for reproducing the pre-call state; short regression examples from ONX-220 have not yet been selected.

## Current constraints

Function declaration resolution, attribute binding, and shape inference must connect local function inputs and outputs, symbolic dimensions, data_prop data propagation, and domain/overload selection, maintaining the element types and shapes that the callerFang Ke sees within the same model; the public element type of the default QuantizeLinear output must explicitly resolve to UINT8.

This requirement means the default quantization type can no longer be recorded as an incidental inference result inside the function. Checks should first confirm the output type that the callerFang Ke sees, then trace back to where attributes and declarations connect; if symbolic dimensions have propagated to the output but the element type has changed to something else, the sample still fails. Conversely, checking only UINT8 while ignoring the caller-visible shape is not enough to establish that cross-layer propagation is complete.

`inf` is a floating-point literal retained in the parser comparison, not a substitute for a function propagation sample. Change only one thing next time: select the shortest real regression from ONX-220, process the same model a second time after completing the first pass, and record results in four areas: inputs and outputs, symbolic dimensions, data_prop, and domain/overload.

## Interface decision

Function text and public protocol: parser.parse_function supports mixing bare names and type declarations in input/output positions, for example `f (float[N] x, spare) => (float[N] y) <float[N] temporary> { temporary = Identity(x) y = Identity(temporary) }` (the function header still declares domain and opset_import). FunctionProto.input/output preserves declaration names and order; type information is stored in repeated ValueInfoProto value_info (wire field 12), covering typed inputs, outputs, and intermediate values in angle brackets before the body, preserving element types, numeric dimensions, and symbolic dimensions; no types are created for unannotated names. value_info associates entries by name and imposes no constraint on list order. Older name-only functions remain valid. NodeProto.overload (field 8) and FunctionProto.overload (field 13), together with domain/name, select the function; helper.make_function supports value_info and the overload parameter. printer.to_text followed by parse_function should preserve these declarations and default attributes. Round-tripping default attributes and node attributes must also preserve scalar types and values (including floats with integer values, negative zero, and strings containing quotes/backslashes/NUL), as well as list types, order, and contents; an explicitly typed empty int/float/string list is also a valid default attribute. # Default Quantization Type Decision Record

This record remains in the old material for the IR-18 compatibility window because “default quantization type” still leads people back here. The earliest decision was narrow: interpret an omitted type as a fixed value so that one node regression sample would still have a clear expected result. Looking back, the real weakness was not whether the sample could run, but that this local judgment was read as a broader policy on types.

The original reading entry point is still `onnx/backend/test/case/node/quantizelinear.py`. The direct dependencies visible in the file are `import numpy as np`, `import onnx`, `from onnx.backend.test.case.base import Base`, and `from onnx.backend.test.case.node import expect`. These pointers lead to the regression sample for QuantizeLinear; they do not list every place that constructs a model or explain how other quantization nodes handle an omitted type.

## The decision built into the sample at the time

Preparation for the window required a decision that could be applied to the existing sample. The draft listed three options: set no default at all; treat every omitted type as an error; or take a default value only from the node case at hand.

The first would leave each call site to interpret the expectation carried by `expect`. The second looked more conservative, but there was no corresponding exception path, error text, or revised sample to support it at the time. The third was therefore adopted: **default quantization type = UINT8.**

The original text also included `zero_point` in the same judgment. As long as the sample fell within the vicinity of this group of quantization inputs, no distinction was made about where the omitted type came from. This kept the regression sample fixed, but whether the type was omitted, whether a zero point was present, and how quantized values were stored were three different questions. The draft did not separate them.

“Wait for confirmation from dependent teams before deciding” was not chosen at the time. That approach would suit a more complete migration review, but it could not answer what the sample should expect that day within the window. The old decision was therefore not a general type inference rule, but a provisional choice for that sample; this limitation was not always visible when the decision was cited later.

## Review notes added in the margin later

This review did not infer implementation ownership from the file location. It only reconfirmed why this page had been retained as an entry point. `quantizelinear.py` provides a node case alongside `Base` and `expect`. That is enough to explain why the old judgment could be included in the regression material, but not enough to establish the full caller scope missing from that judgment.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Read node cases
    Read node cases --> Old window policy
    Old window policy --> Rollback check registration
    Rollback check registration --> Present-day dependency inventory
```

“Rollback check registration” in the diagram corresponds to the `rollback_checked` action recorded later. That action only shows that a check was registered; this page does not retain the rollback target, the check result, or any new type judgment derived from it. It cannot be treated as evidence that “default quantization type = UINT8” has passed a full review, nor can it prove on its own that the old policy has been replaced.

## Branches left incomplete

“Reject if the type is omitted” is still not the decision on this page. The old draft contained no rejection behavior for that path, so retroactively adding it as the approach taken at the time would change the original record. Another reading is to let the presence or absence of `zero_point` directly determine the default type. That was not written as an independent rule either; it was only a mixed judgment left by the draft's treatment of the two together.

The old judgment actually addressed a smaller problem: in the QuantizeLinear regression scenario at the time, the test would not lose its expected result because the type was omitted. It did not address models with an omitted type but nothing corresponding to `zero_point`, nor did it confirm whether the node sample at hand could represent other quantization nodes. The original draft had no answer, and the later review did not add one here.

The present-day dependency inventory is in ONX-206. The card description requires using existing tests or examples to trigger “default quantization type,” then recording uncovered user paths back on the card. It is an entry point for continuing the scope investigation, not an endorsement of the old window's judgment. For the interface-side opset attribute migration, see DOC-20. Both belong to the same compatibility window, but the attribute migration should not be used to supply evidence for the quantization type.

This page therefore retains the original decision and its gaps: UINT8 was the default chosen for the node sample at the time, `zero_point` was folded into the same account by the draft, and coverage was not fully established here. This old policy is not suitable as a new type definition. It is retained so that subsequent inventory work can see why several conditions were combined in the first place.

# opset attribute migration plan

This review will initially center on `onnx/version_converter/adapters/axes_input_to_attribute.h`. The previous investigation led the axes-related issue here, but for now this can only serve as the starting point for examining the adapter object; whether attribute migration also passes through other graph transformation locations has not been verified.

There are two candidate approaches. The first is to retain the old attributes at a later point in the conversion and let the target side or subsequent steps handle them. This involves fewer intermediate graph changes and makes it possible to see whether the old attributes are retained; the issue is that the target and old representations may temporarily coexist. The second is to convert directly to the target representation during adapter processing. This gives downstream code a unified form earlier, but if the target form requires an input while the old model only carries an attribute, migration involves more than changing a field: it also requires deciding where the value comes from and where the input connects.

First, test the second approach with a small graph involving only axes. Record the axis sets before and after conversion, whether the original attribute remains, whether any nodes are added, and whether any new input changes the existing order. A model passing through conversion is not a pass criterion; the meaning of the axes and their dependency positions in the graph must both match.

Do not include other attributes in this trial yet. If the sample requires structure beyond axes to work, or if there is no clear correspondence between the old attribute and the target input, stop this approach and return to the candidate of retaining the old attribute. Record empty axes, explicit axes, and the absence of the attribute separately at first; do not assume they are equivalent.
