# opset Attribute Migration Plan

The original scope is still a class of axes migrations around `onnx/version_converter/adapters/axes_input_to_attribute.h`. This file is useful for tracing back from old issue names, but the path name cannot establish that the entire conversion is completed here. The early draft focused on “whether the attribute was lost”; review found that we also need to examine which stage of the graph callers will see after the attribute lands in the target representation.

The route that retains the old attribute changes the node layout less during conversion. It is suitable for first checking whether the original field is still present, while deferring what the target representation requires. The cost is that part of the graph may simultaneously carry the old attribute and the representation expected on the target side. If later processing does not recognize this mixed state, the problem will only reappear elsewhere.

Migrating directly to the target representation at the adapter looks cleaner. If the old model stores the axis set in an attribute while the target location requires an input, the actual work includes at least: obtaining a usable value from the attribute, deciding whether to reuse an existing source or add a new node, and wiring it into the original node. Any step may make the graph during conversion differ from the graph before conversion. We cannot treat “the attribute names correspond” as evidence that the semantics have been migrated.

## Review clues

The public description of ONX-207 is “the current public entry point supports opset attribute migration.” This helps us continue looking for the entry point, but does not say which attributes or versions are supported, nor whether callers only read the final model or also read the graph during conversion. The card still has one concrete gap: find a caller that still uses this migration and verify the actual version, entry point, and current result.

Therefore, the existence of an entry point is only enough to start a graph-level trial. Without the caller's version and result, we cannot generalize a local conversion into a caller-compatibility conclusion. The earlier judgment that “finding the adapter” meant “we can directly choose when to migrate” was premature.

## Samples to keep separate

axes has at least three recorded states: an explicit set, an explicitly empty set, and the attribute not being provided. An empty set is a value supplied by the model; a missing attribute means the model did not provide that information. There is currently no evidence that they can use the same migration branch for all operators or target opsets.

The trial record should first state the input model's opset, which of these states applies to axes, and whether the graph already has an equivalent value source. On the output side, record where the target representation lands, whether the original attribute is retained, and whether a new node or input dependency appears. If the target form requires an input but no equivalent source can be found, stop here; do not use a default value to disguise a missing attribute as an explicit axis set.

## Trial scope

This time, do not expand this into the entire version-conversion chain. A useful sample only needs to answer: what the axis set expressed before conversion, where it is expressed after conversion, whether a new input changes the node order, and whether the original model is rewritten. Reading the original model back through the old entry point can only check that the input was not damaged by the trial; it does not mean the old entry point should understand the conversion result.

If a caller only consumes the final model, migrating early or late may not expose a difference; if a caller checks the intermediate graph, a new node, a change in input order, or how long the old attribute remains may each become a source of differences. The second type of caller has not yet been found, so neither route can be designated the default on this page.

Attribute field cleanup can be reviewed further under DOC-21, but it is not included in this trial. Migration addresses where the old attribute's semantics go in the target representation; cleanup addresses when the field is removed. Changing both at once would make it impossible to determine whether a difference was caused by input construction, attribute retention, or field cleanup.

# Opset Attribute Migration Proposal

This record preserves a review that was not fully settled during the IR-18 compatibility window; it is not a completed migration description. It originally began with `onnx/version_converter/adapters/axes_input_to_attribute.h`, because the earlier investigation traced axes-related issues to around this adapter. Only during later review was the concern about “whether the old attribute would disappear” separated into two parts: where the target representation belongs, and who would see the change after a new input was added to the graph.

The file path remains an entry point for local verification, not a conclusion about implementation ownership. It can help locate the old adapter and related objects, but it cannot prove that all version conversions pass through here, nor that callers see only the final model. The earlier draft treated the path being nearby as a reason to migrate early; that is no longer accepted.

## Earlier proposals retained here

The first draft listed two approaches. The first was to retain the old attribute at a later point in the conversion and let the target side or a later step handle it. This resulted in fewer changes to the intermediate graph and made it easier to confirm that the old attribute had not yet been dropped. The tradeoff was that the old attribute form and the representation required by the target opset might coexist for some time, and downstream consumers would have to understand this transitional state.

The second was to change to the target representation while the adapter processed the object. Its appeal was that downstream code would receive the same form earlier and would not need to keep checking for the old attribute. However, if the old model provides axes only as an attribute while the target form requires an input, migration is not just a matter of moving the field to another location. We first need to obtain a value equivalent to the old attribute, then determine whether that value comes from an existing node, whether a node must be constructed, and whether connecting the input will alter the original dependency order.

At the time, the preference was to try the second approach first, for a simple reason: if the axis set remains unchanged, unifying the representation earlier makes it easier to read. This old judgment has not been removed because it explains the starting point for the later trial; however, it did not distinguish between final-model consumers and intermediate-graph consumers. The former may care only about the converted semantics, while the latter may observe differences caused by new nodes, input positions, or how long the old attribute remains. The two scenarios cannot be treated as the same result merely because “the conversion succeeded.”

Another old idea was that the process could continue as long as the graph structure did not go beyond the axes-related scope. That boundary is also too coarse. Some graph changes may be required by the target representation itself. What truly requires stopping is not that “a change has appeared,” but that we cannot explain how the change corresponds to the semantics of the old attribute.

## Looking back from the public entry point

The public description for ONX-207 says, “The current public entry point supports opset attribute migration.” It provides a lead for continuing to look for callers and also shows that this discussion should not stop at a single header file. It does not list the attribute set, applicable version combinations, or when callers observe the graph; expanding this sentence into a complete compatibility commitment would be inappropriate.

The unfinished item left on the card is specific: find a caller that still uses this migration and verify the actual version, entry point, and current result. The earlier page phrased “being able to find the entry point” as “being able to choose early migration,” but that wording was later changed. The existence of an entry point only allows the investigation to begin; it cannot replace a caller sample. Without the version, entry point, and result, a graph-level trial cannot be written up as caller compatibility.

The fact that this lead later entered a work-in-progress state does not mean the sample has been completed. The current page has no caller name, actual version, or runtime result that can be recorded, so it retains only candidate approaches. The next time someone finds a usage along ONX-207, that usage’s entry point and the graph stage it received should be added back to this page, rather than filling in a conclusion based on the card title.

## axes must not be treated as one kind of input

During review, the old draft put empty axes and missing axes in the same column. They are now divided into three states:

- Explicit axes: the model provides specific axis values;
- Empty axes: the model explicitly provides an empty set;
- Missing axes: the model does not provide this attribute.

An empty set is not “no information,” and a missing attribute is not “another way of writing an empty set.” This page contains no evidence that these three states have the same migration result for all operators and target opsets. A sample containing only non-empty axes can show only the specific set in that sample; it cannot be used to infer that an empty set and a missing attribute can be filled with the same default input.

Defaults require particular caution. A default might allow the graph to continue being constructed, but it could disguise an originally missing attribute as an explicitly provided axis set. If a difference appears after conversion, we then lose the opportunity to determine whether it came from the old model, input construction, or the way the caller reads the graph. The trial should first record the attribute state, and only then determine whether an equivalent source can be connected to the target location.

An “equivalent source” does not require creating a new branch for every model. It only requires first clarifying exactly what value the target form needs. If an existing node can express the same axis set, its meaning must still be checked when it is reused; if there is no source, a value must not be forced in just to complete the conversion. This stopping point is more useful than asking whether “the model reported an error,” because the latter only shows that the immediate path did not stop.

## What this proposal actually intends to try

The proposal recommends a small, traceable trial, not a batch cleanup of attributes. The sample should make it possible to determine from the model which opset is in use and where axes comes from. At the start, do not mix in other attributes or expand to multiple graph structures; otherwise, when a difference appears after conversion, it will be impossible to distinguish whether it was caused by attribute migration, node construction, or another transformation.

The record can be brief, but it should retain at least the following four areas:

| Location | Information to record |
| --- | --- |
| Before conversion | opset; whether axes is an explicit value, an empty value, or missing; whether the graph already contains a reusable value source |
| After conversion | Where the target representation resides; whether the old attribute is retained; whether additional nodes or input dependencies appear |
| Usage site | The actual entry point; whether it receives the original model, the final model, or the graph being converted |
| Difference location | The first location where the axis set, node order, or input source is observed to be inconsistent |

The “usage site” in the table is still empty and should not be filled with an assumed caller. Without a usage site, the trial may be preserved as a graph-level observation, but it must be kept separate from a compatibility judgment. Being able to read the old model back only checks that the trial did not rewrite the input model; it does not mean that the old entry point needs to understand the target model, much less that the target model preserves the same behavior for all old callers.

For the direct-migration approach, the actions should be split into two steps. First confirm whether the corresponding location in the target opset can still be represented by an attribute; only if it cannot be represented that way should input construction be discussed. After constructing the input, compare it with the axis set expressed by the original attribute. If the value comes from a new node, check where the node was inserted and the input order; if the value comes from an existing node, check that reuse has not caused the existing node to take on a different meaning.

This does not require every adapter to use the same process; it is a local check for this axes trial. It arises from the different locations at which the old attribute and the target input are carried and should not be expanded into a universal statement about all attribute migrations.

## Where each approach loses its basis

The approach of retaining the old attribute is not automatically justified merely because it changes the graph less. Usage sites that consume only the final model may be able to isolate this delay more easily; usage sites that read the intermediate graph may need to observe how long the old representation remains. There is currently no evidence on which to choose between these two scenarios. Even if the final model can be loaded, that does not establish that early and late migration are equivalent for usage sites.

The direct-migration approach cannot be adopted merely because the target representation is more orderly either. When the target form requires an input but no equivalent source can be found, the trial should stop. If a new node changes the input order, first confirm whether any usage site reads that stage; without this information, the change can only be recorded, not declared harmless.

The conditions for withdrawal or pausing are now more specific: do not expand the sample when the correspondence between axes before and after conversion cannot be explained; do not fill in a default value when the target location requires an input but no equivalent source exists; when the node layout on which a usage site depends changes, first confirm which graph stage it reads; if the trial rewrites the original model, stop and save the original model and conversion result separately. The last item comes from the earliest concern about the input being rewritten accidentally and must not be conflated with a backward-compatibility judgment.

If the difference appears only in the final model, first check the axis set and input source, then determine whether it is merely a change in representation location. If the difference has already appeared in the intermediate graph, the read timing itself becomes part of the trial. Without an actual entry point and version, we cannot choose on behalf of the caller whether the migration should happen early or late.

## Keep this separate from attribute-field cleanup

DOC-21 can continue to be used to inspect attribute-field cleanup, but it should not be treated as a follow-up step to this migration. Migration concerns how the semantics of the old attribute are preserved in the target representation; cleanup concerns when the field should be removed. The two changes may be near the same object, or they may have no shared call path. If they are tied together in one trial, then after a failure it will be impossible to attribute the cause to input construction, retention of the old attribute, or field removal.

Therefore, `axes_input_to_attribute.h` remains the local entry point for the earlier investigation. If it is later confirmed that a caller or another adapter participates in graph construction, the record should be updated according to the actual reference relationship rather than continuing to infer from the filename. This page retains the two early approaches and the later narrowing; it does not organize them into the current default migration rule.

There is currently no evidence selecting early or late migration, and there is no caller sample that can be entered on this page. The next addition should first state the actual version and entry point of one usage site, which graph stage it observes, and the result after conversion; if this information still cannot be found, continue to retain the candidate status.

# Attribute Field Cleanup Troubleshooting Tree

## First, Remember What the Symptoms Look Like

This page does not address all attribute issues; it follows the local troubleshooting path left by “attribute field cleanup.” The earliest record started with the issue name and call name and eventually led to `onnx/defs/schema.h`. That destination remains useful, but it can easily lead people to mistake “the file located by the index” for “the file that performs the cleanup.” The actual verification entry point is fixed at revision `v_prev` of `internal/onnx-core`; what this revision provides is local declarations and navigation to adjacent content within the file.

When you encounter the same symptoms, first preserve three things exactly as they are: the attribute name used in the issue, the field spellings that appeared, and the call name that led the investigation here. Do not first combine them into a “schema issue,” and do not retain only a module name. Attribute field cleanup may simply be how the issue is described; these words alone do not establish that cleanup has already occurred near the declaration.

## Why the Old Record Is Still Here

v1 knew only the path entry point, not whether that entry point could explain the full behavior. At the time, it treated `onnx/defs/schema.h` as the first checkpoint, which was a reasonable working hypothesis; however, the file match itself provided no evidence of attributes being deleted, retained, or migrated.

Subsequent maintenance confirmed that the issue name and call name still lead people to this file, so the old entry point cannot be removed. What needs to change is how it is used: first check the local content at the revision containing the path, then decide whether to continue tracing references. Keep the old “start looking here,” but not the old “this is where the processing happens.”

## Entry Point and Record Format

The fixed verification entry point is as follows:

- Repository: `internal/onnx-core`
- Revision: `v_prev`
- Path: `onnx/defs/schema.h`
- Existing search terms: `interop`, `float`, `attributeproto`

These four items keep the review scope fixed on the same file material. The search terms are only indexing clues; even when all three match the same location, that does not mean they belong to the same field cleanup operation. For each match, record at least the following local facts:

- Whether the matched item is a declaration, type name, comment, or adjacent name;
- Whether the attribute name and field name appear there exactly as written;
- Whether the call name appears directly in the file content or was brought in from the old record;
- Whether any local relationship was found that could lead further to the referencing code.

Without these distinctions, the result is merely a record of “a search match was found” and cannot serve as evidence for attributing the cleanup.

## Troubleshooting Tree

```text
When you see an anomaly related to attribute and field cleanup
├─ Can you retain the original attribute name, field name, and call name?
│  ├─ No: stop at input organization first; do not replace fields with general terms
│  └─ Yes: proceed to a local check of schema.h
├─ Is there a match in schema.h for the specified revision?
│  ├─ No: retain the path entry point and record that it was not found; do not replace it with a guess based on the current working tree
│  └─ Yes: distinguish the match type
│      ├─ Declaration or type name only: continue looking for direct references
│      ├─ Adjacent attribute description present: record the adjacency, but do not determine the execution location
│      └─ Call name also appears: compare it word for word with the original symptom
└─ Did you find a reference that can connect to the cleanup action?
   ├─ Yes: record the referenced object and the field it changes
   └─ No: stop at the local declaration and leave an item to verify
```

The purpose of this tree is to separate “path matches,” “adjacency relationships,” and “actual field changes.” If there is no evidence at any level, do not jump to a definite conclusion at the next level.

## Branch 1: The original field can be reproduced

If the incident record still retains the attribute name and field spelling, first search for the corresponding text in `onnx/defs/schema.h`, then check the three frozen matching terms separately. When the attribute name is found, record which declaration it is adjacent to; when it is not found, do not treat the similar `float` or `attributeproto` as the same-named field.

If the three matching terms only provide different adjacency locations, write the locations separately. One location may only be a type declaration, while another may only be a name near an interface. They can help with tracing back together, but they must not be combined in the record as “this is responsible for cleaning up attributes.”

If a direct reference can be seen, put the referenced object, the field read, and the field that changed in the same record. Only when all three line up can the path be advanced from the index entry to the behavior entry. If the field change still cannot be seen, retain “the local declaration was matched, but the cleanup action was not verified.”

## Branch 2: There is only a call name, with no field name

A call name alone is not enough to prove where attribute cleanup occurs. First return to the record that produced the anomaly and confirm whether the call name is from the original text or was relayed by the previous investigator. If the field spelling cannot be recovered, `onnx/defs/schema.h` may be retained as an entry point, but stop short of attributing it to the implementation.

In this branch, do not use any of `interop`, `float`, or `attributeproto` to replace the missing field. They are matching terms already present in the current index, not aliases for the problem field. Once the original field is obtained, restart from Branch 1.

If the call name can be found near the file but there is no corresponding attribute name, record “call name adjacency seen, field relationship not seen.” This is more useful than writing an adjacent declaration as cleanup logic, because the next review can continue directly from the missing relationship without repeating the path lookup.

## Branch 3: Only an attribute-related declaration is matched

When a declaration is matched, first confirm which local object it belongs to, then check whether there are any direct references. Do not infer from the declaration's name that it deletes, renames, or preserves properties. For this page, the minimum result that can be confirmed is: the file at the specified revision contains one local declaration or adjacent object related to the matched term.

If the referencing code can be directly identified from the current material, record the three-part relationship: “declaration—reference—field change”. If only the relationship between the declaration and an adjacent object is visible, record only as far as the adjacent object. If an old record claims this is the processing location, but the corresponding reference cannot be found in this review, retain the old claim as a historical lead while making clear that it has not been confirmed by the current local material.

Do not invent a nonexistent caller to complete a tree branch. When there is no caller, the stopping condition is “declaration located, execution relationship unconfirmed”. This is not a failed investigation, but the boundary of the evidence for that revision.

## Branch Four: Match Results Do Not Align with the Observed Behavior

If `schema.h` does not contain the original property name, or the matched term appears only in an adjacent declaration unrelated to the observed behavior, first confirm that you are checking `v_prev`, then confirm that the path has not been changed to a different file. If both the version and path are correct but the results still do not align, retain the original investigation entry point and state “the observed behavior has not been connected to the local declaration”.

Do not directly overwrite this result with the contents of the current working tree. The current working tree can change the match location and may make old records look more complete, but it cannot establish the relationship for the historical issue in `v_prev`. When a comparison is needed, record the two versions separately; do not retroactively write a match in the newer version as a fact about the older version.

If the reviewer can provide only the issue name and call name, with no fields or references within the file, stop at entry-point verification. When handing off responsibility, include the original term, matched term, repository, version, and path so that the next round does not start again from a generalized “property issue”.

## Handling After Failure

“Recovery” here does not mean arbitrarily modifying properties or deleting fields. Before the execution location is confirmed, do not test a hypothesis by changing schema declarations, changing property names, or deleting adjacent fields. Such actions change the object under investigation and cannot establish which layer produced the original abnormal behavior.

If a review yields only a declaration match, the next step is not to expand the search to the entire project, but to obtain the missing direct references. If a review yields only a call name, the next step is to recover the original field and observed behavior. If the versions are inconsistent, first preserve the version differences, then reassess the match results. If there is insufficient material in all three cases, stop; do not fill the gap with a broader conclusion.

Retaining unsuccessful investigation methods is also valuable: for example, “entered the file using the call name, but did not see a field relationship”. This shows that the entry point is usable and that attribution is not yet complete. If this failure record is deleted, the next maintainer will mistakenly think that the path was never checked.

## revision, Environment, and Local Results

This page references a fixed combination of repository, version, and path. Different working trees, different revisions, or renamed files may all produce different match results for `interop`, `float`, and `attributeproto`. When recording environment differences, include only differences that can be confirmed: repository name, revision, path, matched term, and the object observed.

Do not treat search results in the editor as behavioral results. Search results can show where text is located, but cannot show whether property fields have been cleaned up. Also, do not treat paths recounted in old investigation notes as current reference relationships; they can only explain why this file entry point was retained.

If upstream references need further verification, the handoff should include: the original symptom, property name, field name, call name, file path, revision, the hits for each of the three search terms, and the condition at which the investigation is currently paused. If any item is missing, the next person taking over may only be able to repeat the path search.

## Responsibility Boundaries

Leave the interpretation of local schema declarations and reference relationships to a maintainer who can directly inspect the revision corresponding to `onnx-core`. The public interface owner should confirm the property's meaning in the public interface; the quality owner should confirm the regression behavior, version, and CI results. This page records only the local objects already observed and does not fill in unseen call edges on behalf of any party.

When the issue also involves caller compatibility, the confirmed field changes can be handed off for continued verification during integration testing with the caller, but do not write the caller's assumptions back into the local facts for `schema.h`. Update the attribution on this page only after returning to the same revision and seeing the corresponding references.

## Maintenance Notes

ONX-208 is the navigation entry point for the “property field cleanup” investigation. Its later move into the handling stage indicates that this material is still being used; the card action itself provides no relationships within the file, so a status change cannot substitute for verification results.

This page and the material on strict error propagation address related but separate issues; do not merge the two investigations. This page covers only the entry point, local declarations, reference verification, and stopping conditions for property field cleanup. When another issue name appears, retain it as a routing clue and return to the respective materials.

If the latest verification confirmed only the entry point, not the field changes, the version record should explicitly state “Entry point retained; relationships still pending verification.” If direct references were confirmed, add the specific objects and fields; there is no need to rewrite the preceding historical paragraphs. Keep the old working assumptions in their chronological position in v1, and append new evidence only here.

## Pre-Closure Checklist

- Whether the original property name, field name, and call name can still be reviewed;
- Whether the repository is `internal/onnx-core` and the revision is `v_prev`;
- Whether the path is `onnx/defs/schema.h`;
- Whether the hits for `interop`, `float`, and `attributeproto` are recorded separately;
- Whether declarations, adjacency, and direct references are kept separate;
- Whether a path entry point has mistakenly been recorded as an execution location;
- Whether, when no references are found, the investigation stops at an explicit gap rather than inventing a caller;
- Whether version differences are stored separately from historical materials.

Meeting these conditions only means that this investigation record can be reviewed and verified. It does not turn unseen cleanup actions into known facts, nor does it predetermine the outcome of the next reference check.

## Boundaries of the recorded samples

This page can capture paths, terms, and local relationships, but each type of material supports a different scope of proof. The issue name explains why the file was opened this time; attribute names and field names explain what needs to be retained in the text; call names indicate the direction from which the old record leads into the investigation. Even when they appear together, they cannot be directly combined into the conclusion that “cleanup happened here”. Only when declarations, references, and field changes are visible in the same material is there reason to move from an inspection point toward an entry point for the behavior.

Search results should be retained as they are, rather than first being organized into a conclusion. For each match, at least record the file path, revision, search term, matched object, and whether the investigation can continue to the next step separately. If two terms appear in different locations, mark them separately; if a term appears only in a comment or an adjacent name, accurately record it as adjacent as well. This kind of record may look more fragmented than a single overall judgment, but the next reviewer can use it to determine which relationships have already been examined and which are merely similarities in names.

When encountering objects with similar field names, first retain the original spelling, then check whether the object belongs to the same record as the original symptom. Do not replace a missing field with a broader term, and do not claim that the attribute has been handled merely because `float`, `interop`, or `attributeproto` appears in the file. Search terms serve to narrow the scope of reading; they do not have the authority to turn a declaration into an execution point.

## Comparing two revisions

When comparing an old record with new material, first save the two sides in separate columns. Put only the old issue name, old path, and matches retained at the time on the left; put the files, versions, and local objects currently being viewed on the right. Identical paths do not mean identical contents, and different paths do not mean the old record is invalid. If the current version contains an additional declaration that appears relevant, first state that it appears on the right; do not retroactively write it into the old record's point in time.

A comparison must answer at least three small questions: can the old path still be reproduced today; do the current matches actually connect to a reference; are there observable field changes at the reference site. The three answers may differ. For example, the path may still open, but only a declaration is visible; a reference may also be found without any visible field changes. Recording these asymmetric results makes it easier to continue next time than compressing all three into “confirmed”.

If search output needs to be saved side by side, retain the filenames and match context, and do not treat an editor-filtered summary as the complete material. Context is used only to determine adjacency relationships; it cannot substitute for the actual call site. When no actual call site is currently available, explicitly write “entry point reproduced, call not verified”, and limit the next step to finding a real reference rather than expanding it to the entire repository.

## Minimum material for handoff

When handing this investigation over to someone else, the handoff package should start with a specific sample rather than a module name. Place the original symptom, attribute name, field name, call name, repository, revision, path, and match locations for each search term alongside the sample; if material for any item is unavailable, mark it as not collected. This allows the person taking over to first reproduce the existing entry point, then decide whether the gap concerns field relationships, reference relationships, or caller results.

Do not designate implementation files in advance during handoff, and do not use card status as a substitute for samples. ONX-208 provides navigation only; whichever state it enters cannot prove what kind of change occurred in `schema.h`. If the person taking over can obtain only a path, treat that path as a completed location step and continue looking for references, rather than jumping from “location complete” to “behavior confirmed”.

When there are multiple samples for the same issue, write down the object observed and the stopping point for each sample separately. If one sample hits a declaration and another hits a call, they can provide clues for each other, but they cannot automatically be joined into the same causal chain. Group them under a single relationship only after returning to the same revision to check the intermediate references.

## How to preserve the investigation state when review pauses

When troubleshooting pauses temporarily, retain the last reproducible entry point and the first result that did not match. Do not delete failed search approaches, and do not rewrite “not found” as “this object does not exist”. The former tells the next person how far the search went; the latter can mislead them into thinking the object has already been ruled out. If a review yields only a name, record the name and file location; if it yields a reference but no field change, record the reference and the missing change; if it yields a result but no entry point can be found, explicitly note that the result's source still needs verification.

Follow the same sequence when restoring an old path. First confirm that the old path and old terms can still be revisited, then check whether the new entry point ever had an actual sample, and finally compare the caller-side results. When retracting an overly broad attribution, retract only the attribution text and retain the time and materials documenting that it was checked. This keeps the next round from repeating the same search or treating a failed attribution as a new fact.

The stopping points on this page are always the boundaries of the evidence: if you see a path, stop at the path; if you see a declaration, stop at the declaration; proceed to checking field changes only when you see a direct reference. If new materials become available later, append them after the corresponding stopping point and note which revision they came from. Earlier history is not overwritten when new materials appear; nor should new materials fill in relationships that were absent from the old records at the time.

## Item-by-item checks for handoff records

Before handoff, split each sample into four columns: entry file and revision, actual hit, reproducible direct reference, and changes still awaiting verification. Put them in the same row only when all four columns come from the same search; if only the entry point and hit are available, explicitly write “unverified” in the last two columns rather than filling them in from neighboring files. If the revision changes, retain the old row in its original position, start a new row, and state the differences.

For field cleanup in particular, retain counterexamples. Seeing a property declared does not mean it has been removed from the output; seeing one successful serialization does not mean a rerun after failure will clear temporary state. Reviewers should separately save the observable results for success, rejection, and a subsequent call, and identify which one still lacks a captured investigation state. This lets the next person continue along the gaps without mistaking a navigation aid for a conclusion about the implementation.

# Strict Error Propagation Migration Notes

This page originally contained only a filename and two search terms. After review, `onnx/defs/shape_inference.h` remains a historical reference point, but is no longer described as the sole location responsible for strict error propagation. The old record answers “where to start looking,” not “at which layer the error originates and propagates to the caller.” These two questions must be recorded separately; otherwise, as long as the directory remains unchanged, later readers can easily mistake the reference location for an implementation entry point that has already been migrated.

The old investigation started with the issue name “strict error propagation” and used `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror` to find that header file. Keeping this information as it was serves a practical purpose: the issue name identifies the behavior being checked at the time, the search terms identify the local areas that were opened, and the file path preserves a location to revisit. If any of these three is missing, later readers will have to guess again why the old record stopped here.

## What the Old Entry Point Means

`onnx/defs/shape_inference.h` is the old reference path, not an automatically inferred new path. The old record is associated with existing material for `internal/onnx-core`; when the file was accessed through the issue name and call name, only declarations and their adjacency were visible. The filename alone cannot establish that the error originates in shape inference, nor can it establish that the caller directly depends on this file. The migration record should preserve this limited scope rather than add an execution chain that the old investigation never found.

The old entry point therefore retains two uses. The first is to revisit the declaration scope containing `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror`, to confirm whether the new search still starts from the same objects. The second is to place failure output obtained later alongside the old record for comparison: did the old record merely match a name, or did it already point to a location that could explain the output? Both uses require the path to exist, but neither requires the path to be presented as a conclusion about behavior.

The old entry point does not serve a third purpose: it cannot replace an actual call. Without a call location, we do not know how `strict_mode` enters the current scenario; without the result seen by the caller Fang Ke, we do not know whether `inferenceerror` is the error the user sees; without the runtime environment, we cannot determine whether a failure to reproduce is due to a change in the path, the input, or the environment. The old file can still be opened, but being able to open it does not mean the migration is complete.

## First, Define What Is Being Migrated

What is being migrated here is not the header file, nor is this a matter of replacing one search term with another. The migration concerns an investigation and verification path: it starts from the old issue name, passes through a declaration location that can be revisited, and ends at a strict-mode call that can be checked again. The new path is established only after that call has been recorded.

When recording the new path, at least the following information needs to be kept in one place:

- The original issue name that prompted the check;
- The actual location where the call enters;
- Whether there is any wrapping or conversion before the call;
- How strict mode appears in this call;
- Where the error becomes the result seen by the caller Fang Ke;
- What role the old path still plays in the comparison.

This does not require filling in a complete call graph first. The current material provides neither a complete call graph nor a sample that can be rerun directly. This ordering is simply intended to prevent “found a declaration” from being misrecorded as “found the user entry point.” If only one item has been confirmed, record only that item and leave the others unfilled.

The old record places `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror` together because they jointly formed the initial search scope; the specific control relationship between them has not been confirmed by the material on this page. In subsequent reviews, do not interpret one as a switch and the other as the final error merely because their names appear next to each other. First record which declarations each appears near, then use an actual call to establish whether both participate in the same path.

## Order of Migration Away from the Old Path

First open the old path and record the local declarations currently visible and the immediate adjacency of the two search terms. The output of this step should be a location description that can be revisited, not an architecture diagram filled in from the directory hierarchy. If `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror` have no direct relationship within the current viewing scope, record that accurately as well; this will prevent later records from combining two independent matches into a definite conclusion.

The second step is to find an actual call. What needs to be recorded is not an abstract statement that “strict mode is used somewhere,” but where this call comes from, what context is passed in, whether it goes through a wrapper first, and how the result it returns or throws reaches the caller. This page currently has no such call sample, so this step remains empty. Until a sample is found, names in the header file cannot stand in for how the call is made.

Only in the third step should the old record and the new path be compared. In the comparison, first ask whether the old path still explains the declaration location in the new material; then ask whether the new call actually passes through that location; finally, ask whether the result seen by the caller is the same as the error originally being checked. The answers to these three questions may differ. For example, the new call may still use the same declaration scope but expose the error to the caller through a different wrapper; alternatively, the old path may retain only its search value, with the new call never passing through it at all. The migration record needs to accommodate both outcomes.

Only in the fourth step should caller documentation be changed. There is currently no frozen list of callers and no migration batch that can be confirmed, so this page must not invent entities that have already switched over. Once a call has been obtained, first attach it under the new path as an individual sample; group calls into a batch only after multiple calls have been confirmed one by one. A batch is a recording unit used later when organizing callers, not a label for filling the current gap.

```text
Old issue name
   |
   +-- `strict_mode` / `inferenceerror`
   |          |
   |          v
   |   onnx/defs/shape_inference.h
   |          |
   |          +-- Declarations and adjacency: can be revisited
   |
   +-- Actual strict-mode call: to be added
                  |
                  +-- Wrapper location: to be added
                  +-- Caller result: to be added
```

“To be added” in the diagram is not a candidate module name. It means that the old record did not retain enough material to fill in that node. When adding nodes later, start from the actual call and fill in both directions: upward with the call's source, and downward with the result seen by the caller. Do not start guessing from adjacent directories or similarly named files, because that would turn navigation information back into an attribution judgment.

## Comparisons to Preserve During Review

The old path, the new call, and the error result should be included in the same comparison, but they do not need to be disguised as a continuous causal chain. The recommended recording method is to write the old reference point first, then the call sample, and finally paste in the caller result; distinguish the three using “confirmed” and “not yet confirmed.” This way, even if the new call is later shown to belong to another layer, the value of the old record's declaration location will not be damaged.

The original issue name is the easiest thing to lose in the comparison. Later readers will often search directly for `strict_mode` or `inferenceerror`, then treat the search results as the issue itself. The original issue name should remain at the start of the record because it shows that this check concerns strict error propagation, not every location containing these two strings. Search terms can broaden the search scope; they cannot replace the issue scope.

The second thing that is easily lost is the context of the old revision. The old path comes from an existing record, and the version of the material on which it was based should be preserved when reviewing it, to avoid automatically projecting adjacent content in the current tree back onto the old conclusion. This does not require creating a new version note for every browsing session; simply noting beside the new call whether it and the old reference point come from the same material lets later readers know that the two sides of the comparison are not inherently identical.

The third thing that is easily lost is the result seen by the caller. An error name, an exception object, and user-facing text may not be the same thing. This page currently preserves no specific output, so it cannot prescribe in advance what the result should look like. When adding samples, the raw result takes priority over an edited overview; if only an overview can be obtained, make clear that it establishes only that someone observed the issue, not the layer where the error first appeared.

## Counterexamples and Stopping Points

After finding a candidate call, do not immediately record it as the new entry point. At least two cases need to be distinguished: a call that enters strict mode but does not produce the error being checked, and a call that enters the same kind of scenario and does produce that error. Neither type of input is provided here, so they must not be invented as regression samples; however, the record template should reserve entries for both, to avoid treating any strict-mode call as the target entry point based only on failures.

The value of a counterexample is that it narrows attribution. If a call finishes normally in strict mode, it at least reminds us that the name “strict mode” alone cannot explain the error. If another call produces an error but has an additional wrapper layer in its path, the difference cannot be attributed directly to the header file either. First examine the locations each of the two calls passes through, then determine which difference is worth pursuing further.

When there is no comparable counterexample, the migration can stop at “candidate call found.” This status is more useful than “migration complete” because it tells the next review what to bring back: a call that can fail, a call suitable for comparison, and the paths from each to its caller result. Do not mark inputs that have not been run as passing or failing just to complete the table.

If the new call establishes only the entry location but does not explain the error result, record it as “call located, propagation unverified.” If there is only an error result and no reliable call location, record it as “result collected, entry point unverified.” If both are available but it is still unclear whether strict mode actually participates, record it as “call and result collected, mode relationship unverified.” These statuses can coexist across different samples and should not be compressed into a generic completion level.

## While the Old and New Paths Coexist

Do not delete the historical reference path `onnx/defs/shape_inference.h` during migration. Once a new entry point is found, add it as a new paragraph after the old path, and state clearly whether it is a call entry point, a wrapper location, or an observation point for the caller result. This allows readers to return from the old issue name to the earliest declaration location, while also following the added material to see how far subsequent additions have progressed.

If the new entry point and the old path ultimately point to the same place, retain both names: the old path explains how it was found at the time, and the new entry point explains how its participation in the call was later verified. If the two are no longer the same, there is still no need to delete the old path; note beside it that it is used only for historical comparison, and identify the new actual call separately. Deleting the old path would mislead later readers into thinking the earlier record never existed, while retaining it without distinguishing its purpose would cause the opposite misunderstanding.

Changes to caller documentation should come after this step. There is currently no set of callers to register, so this page specifies only the recording order: first confirm an individual call, then confirm whether it represents a category of callers, and only then revise the caller-facing migration notes. If the notes are changed first and calls added later, it is easy for the notes to contain “switched over” judgments that cannot be traced back.

For experimental material related to metadata boundaries, see [DOC-23](DOC-23). It can help readers locate another record within the same compatibility window, but it cannot supply this page with call samples for strict error propagation. Keep the inputs, results, and conclusions of the two records separate, to avoid mixing unrecorded observations merely because the topics are adjacent.

## How to Restore the Old Path

Restoring the old path does not mean erasing all newly added content. If a newly added entry point later fails to reproduce the old issue, first withdraw the description that labels it as the migration target, while preserving the record that the entry point was checked and the results obtained at the time. Keep the old reference path, the original issue name, `strict_mode`, and `inferenceerror`, because they are the starting points for locating the issue again next time.

After restoration, recheck in the original order: whether the local declarations at the old path can still be revisited; whether the new call was actually recorded; whether the caller result comes from that same call; and whether strict mode is merely a search clue or has already been shown by a sample to participate. These checks do not require reinterpreting the entire module; they are intended to prevent a mistaken attribution from leaving behind text that is harder to deal with than the original gap.

If the new material changed only the reference location and did not change caller documentation, restoration requires only withdrawing the attribution judgment for the new location. If caller documentation already refers to the new entry point, first change it back to “call sample pending verification,” then remove statements such as “migration complete.” The old file path should not be used as a rollback target to replace code; this page preserves investigation paths and relationships between materials, not code modification instructions.

Once restoration is complete, retain only a brief explanation of the reason for failure, such as “the candidate call could not be matched to the original result” or “the wrapper location has not yet been confirmed.” Do not rewrite a sample that could not be matched into a new overall judgment. It only means that the sample cannot currently serve as the migration entry point; it may still provide a comparison for the next search.

## Evidence from the Actual Scenario Still to Be Added

The current gaps are concentrated in the following items:

- The most recent actual call and its entry location;
- Whether the call passes through wrapping or conversion;
- The raw error result seen by the caller;
- The version and runtime environment corresponding to that result;
- A strict-mode counterexample that can be distinguished from the failing call;
- Whether an actual reference relationship exists between the old reference point and the new call;
- Whether the confirmed callers are sufficient to form a migration batch.

Until this material is available, `onnx/defs/shape_inference.h` remains a useful historical entry point, and `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror` remain usable search points; none of them constitutes evidence that the migration of strict error propagation has been completed. The next addition to the record should start with an actual call and append the newly obtained content after the existing path on this page.

# Final-component symlink trial proposal

Within the IR-18 compatibility window, final-component symlinks are being considered separately because they cannot be folded into the same path rule as parent-directory handling. Here, “final component” means only the last path component corresponding to the external data filename; whether parent directories are reached through symlinks is not being settled in this interface review.

The initial view is to put the decision point near the interface that opens external data, rather than have each reader interpret paths on its own. The reason is not to reorganize all external data flows. It is simply that once a caller resolves a symlink ahead of time, the subsequent open operation can no longer see the original boundary.

There are two candidate approaches.

- The reader checks the supplied path text first, then decides whether to proceed with opening it.
- The helper interface responsible for opening external data retains the final-component object and returns an accept or reject result.

The first looks like a smaller change, but the same model could get different decisions at different call sites. The second requires checking whether the interface can cover the existing read paths, but it centralizes the decision and makes it easier to place regression samples at the same point.

For this round, the recommendation is to try only the second approach. The trial does not require handling parent-directory symlinks first, nor does it move ordinary external files to a different entry point. Prepare one ordinary external file and one sample whose final component is a symlink, and check whether both open operations still go through the same helper layer.

Still undecided: what form a rejection should take for the caller; whether reading and saving share the same boundary; and who should interpret an ordinary path that contains a symlink name but whose final component is not a symlink. If the trial forces callers to reconstruct paths themselves, withdraw the idea of consolidating the interfaces and retain the existing read paths.

The first draft focused on “don't make callers decide for themselves.” After review, that direction can still stand, but the original wording was too broad: not every path-related case needs to be brought into one interface. This round only covers the final-component object of an external data file. Ordinary external files and parent-directory symlinks remain open to their own discussions.

Start the code review at `onnx/external_data_helper.py`. The file header shows direct dependencies on `os`, `re`, `sys`, and `uuid`; this only establishes that the file is a suitable checkpoint for external data helper logic, not that all path policy belongs there. Investigation entries are concentrated in ONX-212; continue from there to locate further samples and rules.

The candidate approach is now split into three layers rather than an either-or choice:

1. Callers perform text checks. This layer can still provide early warnings, but should not be the sole basis for deciding how to handle final-component symlinks.
2. The external data open interface retains the actual open operation. The trial should sit at this layer and verify that acceptance or rejection of the final-component object does not vary by call site.
3. Track directory-level symlinks separately. If a path has already passed through a parent-directory symlink before reaching the final-component object, move it into the scope of DOC-26, rather than use this proposal to add a blanket “reject all symlinks” rule.

The trial samples must distinguish at least two things: ordinary external files continue to enter the helper layer as usual; files whose final component is a symlink receive explicit handling at the same layer. Records should include the model directory, the relative location of the external data, and the read branch actually taken. Recording only “symlink failed” is not useful: that observation cannot distinguish whether the cause was a parent directory, path joining, or the final object.

# Trial proposal for final-component links

This was initially framed as a small interface question: when an external data path reaches its last name, should the caller first check whether it is a link? That framing later proved insufficient. The caller sees a string; the open operation sees the object. If resolution has already happened between the two, the final-component boundary can easily be erased before the open operation.

Final-component links are not a stand-in for the security policy for the entire path, though. This proposal covers only the last path component of external data files within the model directory. It does not add rules for traversal through links in parent directories, legacy behavior for ordinary directory links, or cases where callers explicitly resolve the path beforehand. Parent-directory cases remain tracked separately in DOC-26, so the same sample does not get interpreted independently on two pages.

## Direction retained from the first draft

The first draft proposed having readers check the incoming path before entering the helper layer. The benefit at the time was straightforward: changes would be concentrated at a few call sites, and failures could return earlier. That proposal is retained here because it explains why the initial review favored text checks.

But that recommendation is no longer part of the trial. Path text can only express the name supplied by the caller; it cannot replace a check of the final object. If each reader implements its own check, final-component links become a caller convention rather than a boundary of the external data interface. This problem usually does not show up with regular-file samples; link samples are needed to expose it.

The first draft also said, “All links are handled by the same interface.” That statement has been discarded. It conflated the directory layer with the final object and implied that the save side would automatically follow the read side. There is not enough evidence to support either extension.

## Focus after review

The starting point for rechecking remains `onnx/external_data_helper.py`. This file directly imports `os`, `re`, `sys`, and `uuid`, making it a useful place to continue inspecting adjacent external data handling code. The import list itself does not establish a directory policy or which callers are responsible. ONX-212 remain navigation references for observed samples and rule locations; the investigation steps on those cards are not repeated here.

This trial is scoped to `_open_external_data_fd`. external_data_helper provides the `_open_external_data_fd` interface, which uses file descriptors to safely open external data files within the model directory and rejects symbolic links. Discussion of final-component links should center on this interface: rather than first committing to path rewrites in every caller, confirm whether the final open point can retain and enforce this boundary.

Here, “rejects symbolic links” refers specifically to the final object covered by this page. If a sample has already traversed a parent-directory link before reaching that object, do not use this conclusion to count the parent directory as covered too. That would make it impossible during investigation to tell which layer rejected the path.

## What this round tests

The trial compares only two types of samples: regular external data files in the model directory, and external data files whose final object is a symbolic link. The former checks that consolidating the interfaces has not rerouted normal reads through a bypass; the latter checks that caller-side path preprocessing has not swallowed the check. Records should retain the model directory, the relative location of the external data, the helper interface entered, and the return status. Writing only “links cannot be read” is not enough to tell whether the issue lies in the final component, a parent directory, or caller-side path construction.

Leaving the save side out of this round is deliberate. Path generation during saving, handling of existing files, and the open operation during reading do not necessarily share the same boundary. Once the read-side samples are stable, decide whether the save side needs an interface with the same name or only needs to retain the existing restrictions. Changing both sides together would make it hard during rollback to tell which side changed regular-file behavior.

Nor are callers required to migrate to a single pattern. The trial first checks whether existing read paths can reach this interface. If a read point does bypass it, record that point and the object it passes in, then discuss whether routing it through the interface is worthwhile. There is no reason to turn one review of final-component links into a plan to rework all external data callers.

## Trade-offs

Text prechecks still have value, especially when callers want to provide their own message earlier. But they can only serve as an additional hint, not replace the check at the final open point. Placing the check near the open interface means having to verify that the interface actually covers the target read paths. The benefit is that the same final object will not be handled differently depending on the caller.

Another approach would be to first establish a set of path rules covering directories, filenames, and save behavior, then derive interfaces from those rules. That approach is not being adopted at this stage. It would bring parent-directory links, regular external files, and unresolved save-side questions into the same review. The review scope would be too broad, and the two sample types available here would not be enough to judge success.

## Stop conditions

If any of the following occurs, do not use this proposal to proceed with broader changes:

- A regular external data file takes a different read branch because of the final-component check;
- Identifying the final object requires every caller to resolve the full path itself first;
- Samples show that the issue actually comes from a parent-directory link rather than the last path component;
- The interface cannot explain whether it handles opening or saving, yet is expected to carry the semantics of both.

Stopping does not mean reverting to the old “each caller checks for itself” approach. First retain the samples and the branches they entered, then move parent-directory cases back to the corresponding page and leave the save side unresolved. Only if final-component samples and regular-file samples can be distinguished at the same helper interface should the next discussion cover error forms, caller adaptation, and a fixed location for regression samples.

Only three specific questions remain to be confirmed: which existing read paths enter `_open_external_data_fd` directly; what information the upper layers need to retain on rejection; and whether saving external data can encounter the same final object. These do not affect this round's proposal to keep final-component link handling near the open interface, but they will determine whether the trial can move from a limited set of samples to a stable change.

versions.body:
# Parent Directory Link Troubleshooting Tree

The earliest record on this page covered a very narrow scenario: the model and external data were unchanged, but after the parent directory changed from a regular directory to a link, the status returned by the discovery entry point changed. The value of the old draft was not that it had already explained the cause, but that it required preserving the original relative path. Later, some people called final-component file links, missing files under regular directories, and parent directory links all “link issues,” which instead led this record off track.

We still start from `onnx/external_data_helper.py`, but do not treat this filename as an attribution of the cause. The old troubleshooting record landed here based on the issue name and call name; the file shows direct dependencies on `os`, `re`, `sys`, and `uuid`, but that does not establish which branch is responsible for handling the path. The incident record should first establish the inputs and statuses, then decide whether to continue investigating along the call relationships.

ONX-213 preserves only the local verification of this parent directory link: pass the path through the current file discovery entry point, and retain the relative path and the status returned by the tool. The card itself did not explain the difference as a conclusion about a particular function, so this page does not describe it as an implementation defect that has already been located either.

## Separate the cases first

Here, “parent directory link” means that a directory component before the filename in the relative external data path is a link. For example, the input under the model directory is a relative path, and an intermediate directory in that path is not a regular directory. This differs from the following two scenarios:

- The filename itself is a link, and all parent directories are regular directories;
- The path contains no links, but the target file does not exist, permissions are insufficient, or the model directory has already changed.

The three cases may produce the same failure status, or they may produce different statuses. Identical statuses do not prove that the same processing path was taken; different statuses also cannot be explained away simply by saying “the link was rejected.” The old draft was too optimistic on this point: it treated the parent directory link as the only variable, but the actual record did not preserve enough control inputs.

First copy down these four items; if any one is missing, do not continue guessing:

1. The path of the directory containing the model, as observed in the incident;
2. The original relative path passed to the discovery entry point;
3. Which parent directory in the path is a link, rather than just writing “contains a link”;
4. The status returned by the tool or the original error text.

The original relative path matters. Collapsing it in advance, changing it to an absolute path, or manually eliminating `.` and `..` before recording it will erase the differences needed for this check. This does not require classifying every component in the path as safe or unsafe; it only requires letting later readers know what the tool saw.

## Incident branches

```text
Obtain the model directory, relative path, and status
|
+-- The parent directory in the path is not a link
|   |
|   +-- The filename is a link
|   |   `-- Go to the final-component link record; do not apply this page's conclusions.
|   |
|   `-- No links
|       `-- First check it as a regular external file. If you need to compare against old migration records, see DOC-27.
|
`-- The parent directory in the path is a link
    |
    +-- The original relative path was not saved
    |   `-- Stop attributing the cause; first add the original path and the status returned by the tool.
    |
    +-- A regular-directory control exists for the same model and the same relative path
    |   |
    |   +-- Both statuses are the same
    |   |   `-- The parent directory link has not produced a recorded difference; check the target file and model directory.
    |   |
    |   `-- The statuses differ
    |       `-- Save both statuses and the directory conditions; continue checking the path received by the discovery entry point.
    |
    `-- No regular-directory control exists
        `-- Record only “status when the parent directory is a link”; do not describe it as a reproduced boundary rule.
```

This tree has more stopping points than the old version. Previously, as soon as the parent directory was seen to be a link, the investigation would continue focusing on the link itself; this turned incidents without controls into definite conclusions. Now, if the original relative path or a comparable regular-directory condition is missing, the record stops at “what was returned under this condition.” It can still be used for later verification, but not for a release decision.

## Do not reverse the order

During troubleshooting, first ask where the path was passed to the discovery entry point, then ask where it ultimately points in the file system. The former is a local fact this page can preserve; without a control from the same incident, the latter can easily be replaced by the result of manual resolution. Successfully opening the target file manually also does not mean that the tool will reach the same location using the same relative path.

Use two lines in the record rather than a single summary sentence:

```text
Relative path passed in: <preserve the original text>
Status returned by the tool: <preserve the original text>
```

If the parent directory is a link, add another line identifying which directory component is the link. Do not insert the target's final location back into the first line. This is not about collecting more path details, but about avoiding recording “what the input is” and “what the file system ultimately resolves it to” as the same object.

When comparing against a regular directory, do not change multiple conditions either. Keep the model directory, relative path, and target file the same; change only the parent directory's directory condition. If you also change the filename, external data contents, or model location while constructing the control, the result can only be treated as a separate incident and should not overwrite the original record.

The old page contained an informal practice: first replace the linked directory with a regular directory, then see whether the problem disappears. This can help obtain a control while on call, but it is not a recovery action, much less an instruction authorizing changes to user directories. If the status changes after replacement, that only shows that the tool returns different results under the two directory conditions; if the status remains unchanged after replacement, that only rules out an obvious difference in this particular comparison. The old draft described “unchanged” as “unrelated to the link”; that judgment is retained here, marked as no longer applicable.

> Deprecated old judgment: If a regular directory and a parent directory link produce the same status, the path boundary can be considered uninvolved.
>
> Correction: Identical statuses do not show that the two paths underwent the same processing. Without more incident evidence, record only that the statuses are the same; do not infer that the internal steps are the same.

## What to check near the discovery entry point

When the comparison does show a status difference, first confirm that the difference occurs at the “current file discovery entry point” layer, rather than appearing only after the model directory has been replaced. This does not require incident responders to read the entire helper; they only need to compare the relative path passed at the call site with the original text in the record. If the string at the call site is no longer the same, the parent directory link is merely an observed condition and can no longer be treated as the sole variable.

Then ask the following questions in order:

- Does the call site supply a relative path, or a path that has already been converted?
- Is the model directory in the record still the directory from which the model was originally loaded?
- Is the link in a parent directory, or is it actually the final filename?
- Does the tool status appear during discovery, or only during the subsequent read stage?

The last item is often the easiest to omit. If all you know is “cannot open,” you cannot tell whether the discovery entry point has already been passed. Do not describe a general file-read failure as a parent directory link failure just to complete the record; the two must be distinguished using the same set of inputs and statuses.

If the path supplied by the call site has already been converted, this page stops at the call site. Continuing to speculate about directory handling inside `onnx/external_data_helper.py` adds no new facts at this point. Saving the before-and-after strings side by side is more useful than adding an explanation. If the two are completely identical, return to the comparison between the parent directory link and the regular directory.

## Three easy wrong turns

**Treating a final-component link as a parent directory link.** When the filename is a link, all directory components in the path may still be regular directories. The old issue record covered only the parent directory condition; appending final-component link results here would mislead later readers into thinking that both entry points had already been checked.

**Rewriting the relative path first.** Some people habitually construct an absolute path before reproducing the issue to make it easier to inspect the target manually. This action can be included as a note, but it cannot replace the value passed in. The current card requires preserving the relative path and the status returned by the tool precisely because rewriting the path makes it impossible to see the input presented to the discovery entry point.

**Calling a single regular-directory test a fix.** A regular-directory control only helps determine whether the difference changes with the directory condition. It does not establish that links should be accepted, nor does it establish that links should be rejected. The old version's “replace it with a regular directory and you can continue” applied only to the sample temporarily retained at that time; it should not be carried over to other models or directory structures.

Of these three, the first remains the most common recording error; the second makes the record lose its verification value; the third misrepresents a control action as an operational recommendation.

## The minimum snippet to retain during verification

When incident information is incomplete, leave a short snippet rather than inventing directory details:

```text
Model directory: <value visible in the incident>
Relative path: <original text>
Parent directory link: <directory component or unconfirmed>
Tool status: <original text>
Regular-directory control: present / absent; if present, status is <original text>
```

“Unconfirmed” is not a failure record. It means that this check cannot yet distinguish a parent directory link from other directory conditions. Conversely, if the record contains only a status and no original path, do not write “parent directory link anomaly” in the title or conclusion either; at most, label it a path difference pending verification.

After ONX-213 entered processing, the relative path and status under the current discovery entry point were added back, but no new conclusions were added about final-component links, file contents, or model format. This page therefore retains its old narrow scope: it supports rechecking parent directory conditions, not handling every external data failure.

## Stopping conditions that still apply

Troubleshooting on this page can end when any one of these conditions is met:

- The current path is confirmed not to contain a parent directory link; go to the regular external file record.
- A final-component file link is confirmed; do not continue applying the parent directory branch.
- A parent directory link exists, but the original relative path or tool status is missing; complete the record before making a judgment.
- The comparison between the regular directory and the parent directory link has been saved, and it can be clearly stated whether the two statuses are the same or different; hand the evidence over for verification at the call site.

Do not append an overall judgment of “links are safe” or “links are unsafe” at the end. The available evidence only supports preserving conditions, inputs, and statuses separately. The path entry point in the old workflow still has reference value, especially when reviewing whether a relative path was rewritten; all other conclusions should be based on new evidence from the call site.
